title: 10.04 Spatial transcriptomics identifies metabolic dysregulation as a key driver of T cell exclusion in esophageal adenocarcinoma
abstract: Background Success of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) in esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is dependent on the level of activation of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Patients with a complete pathological response ((pCR), 20% of EACs) have higher intratumoral CD8 T cell levels and a higher CD8:CD163 ratio compared to patient with a non-pCR. To improve response to nCRT we have to identify and target the mechanism EACs use to keep CD8 T cells out. Materials and Methods To this end we used tissues of patients with high vs. low intratumoral CD8 T cell density (multiplex immunohistochemistry) from a previous study for spatial whole transcriptomics (Nanostring GeoMx DSP) to characterize the transcriptome of cancer cells in CD8 high vs. low tumor areas. Regions of interest (ROI) were determined based on T cell density (CD3+) and analyzed for whole transcriptome of both tumor cells (PanCK+) and adjacent immune cells (CD45+) separately. Transcriptional differences were validated using bulk transcriptome data from publicly available data bases (TCGA) and Single Cell ENergetIc metabolism by profiling Translation inhibition (SCENITH) using fresh resection material (n=4). Results Whole transcriptome analyses of CK+ ROIs (cancer cells) identified that they clustered separately based on T cell infiltration status, indicating that CK+ cells in inflamed EACs are transcriptionally distinct from those in non-inflamed EACs. Differential gene analysis showed that antigen presentation pathway genes (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, and B2M) were upregulated in CD8-high EACs, whereas tumors with CD8-low EACs overexpressed genes associated with attraction and M2-like polarization of macrophages, such as IDO1, CXCL5, and CSF2. Differential pathway analyses indicated that the largest difference between CD8-high and CD8-low EACs was related to lipid metabolism. CD8 high tumors show high activity of immune pathways, such as antigen presentation and IL7 signaling, whereas the CD8 low tumors were characterized by high activity of the HDL and chylomicron remodeling pathways. Pathway analysis of the CD45+ compartment identified upregulation of the PGC1a pathway in CD8 T cell low tumors, a known driver of mitochondrial biogenesis and associated with suppressive myeloid cells. The correlation between CD8 T cell status and mitochondrial metabolism was confirmed by publicly available transcriptional data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) showing high OXPHOS and fatty acid oxidation to be associated with low cytolytic scores. Using single cell metabolic analysis (SCENITH) on fresh tumors we confirmed the presence of OXPHOS dependent myeloid cells in the TIME of CRT resistant EACs. Conclusions Comparative analyses of tumor transcriptomes from CD8 T cell rich vs. poor areas reveal an association between downregulation of antigen presentation and chemo attraction of suppressive myeloid cells and low CD8 T cell infiltration. Furthermore, we found dysregulation of lipid metabolism in both tumor and immune cell compartments as a potential driver of immune suppression and T cell exclusion in EAC. J. Sanders: None. E.N. title: A Full Life in a Small Place by Janice Emily Bowers
abstract: Reviews 243 three Mexican outlaws. The story is told from her point of view, and the psychological realism is astounding. The reader shares in the whole gamut of her complex response to her experience, from the fear and hatred of the first few days to the emotional numbing ofthe long captivity time to the beginnings of healing and forgiveness at the end. Although young Bernardino, who has befriended her, eventually brings her home, things do not end happily. If you have read nothing by R. G. Vliet, do so. Until that time, your education in the literature of the American West is incomplete. CHARLOTTE M. WRIGHT University ofNorth TexasPress A Full Life in a Small Place. ByJanice Emily Bowers. (Tucson: University of Arizona Press, 1993. 166 pages, $24.95/$13.95.) The pages ofJanice Emily Bowers’ A Full Life in a Small Place are few in number, but the book is bigger. Much. The single thread on which this collec­ tion ofessaysisstrung isthe author’sgarden in Tucson, Arizona, and, assuredly, by the final page the reader knows her garden well enough to see, smell, and taste it.Anyone interested in the details ofgardening in a harsh, desert location can read, enjoy, and profitfrom the book. Bowers,whose other titles are A Sense of Place and The Mountains Next Door; is a botanist with the U.S. Geological Survey, and writes clearly about matters botanical. But, in prose of not only clarity, but ofgrace, Bowers draws texts from her small garden that are as big as the world itself: predation (“Nature is profligate with life. Far from being sacred, it is the most expendable of commodities, as disposable as feathers or fingernails”); the physicality of pleasure (“I once believed that the sweetest words in English were thetideis out. . . but now I think that vineripened tomatoes comes close, maybe even surpasses them”); extrapolation (“. . . gardens are placeswhere the gardener engages the outside world in a continuing conversa­ tion”); understanding (“Data should never pass for wisdom”). In addition she has written one of the finest concise overviews of insect senses I’ve ever read. The essay entided ‘The Eye of the Dragonfly” is a gem, worth the price of admission all by itself. Bowers is too conscious an environmentalist not to be bothered by making a garden in anybut the desert’sownway, that isseasonallyand with plants other than the dry land’s own moisture misers. In a place where growing human populations are using water at a rate exceeding replenishment, her sunflowers and broccoli make her feel unrighteous: If I grow thirsty plants like zucchini and watermelon, am I living as if water mattered? I offer trade-offs to salve myconscience. What ifI take 244 Western American Literature a shower every other day instead of daily? What if I wash my car only once a month—or never? Shouldn’t it be permissable to grow veg­ etables ifI don’t have a lawn? IfI build up the soilwith compost, itwill retain more water, and I’ll need to irrigate less often. At least I dig my garden by hand; I’m not pouring fossil fuels into a gasoline-powered rototiller. Oh, I turn cartwheels in my efforts to rationalize this desert garden. In turn, of course, the reader in other climates, wetter perhaps, but lacking in some other way, must reflect on the human use ofother resources at excessive rates on the personal, industrial, and governmental level. Perhaps a few extra buckets ofwater more than her share can be permitted toJanice EmilyBowersif she can help the rest ofus think these thoughts. SUE HUBBELL Southern Missouri Ozarks (and) Washington, D. C. Songs of My Hunter Heart: A Western Kinship. By Robert F. Gish. Drawings by Kenyon Thomas. (Ames: Iowa State University Press, 1992. 150 pages, $21.95.) This book with the beautiful title is the story of a hunter growing up—and thus outgrowing hunting (something that Hemingway and a lot of other hunt­ ers never achieved). It is a well-wrought collection of youth-coming-of-agethrough -hunting stories from the writer’sown youth. The best part isthe strong characterization and feelings ofaffection generated among the familymembers and friends who participate in the stories...

title: Yellow Canaries
abstract: 52 Yellow Canaries Donna G. Akers Slowly flexing her gossamer wings, the dragonfly, or witch doctor as Granny called it, contentedly perched on the edge of the washtub. I gently splashed water at her and she flitted high into the air. It sure was late in the year for witch doctors to still be out. Sinking my hands back into the tub of dirty laundry, I kept squeezing and swishing the clothes around. From here on the porch I could keep an eye on my younger brothers and sisters. Mama had told me that's the job of the oldest child. Gazing out in the yard, I saw the kids chasing each other along the creek banks where the autumn leaves had begun to nest. Old man winter could be here soon. Mama says the caterpillars already have woolly coats, meaning we're going to have a hard, cold winter. After hanging the clothes on the clothesline strung between the two tulip trees, I herded up the kids and made them wash up at the outdoor spigot before supper. As we tumbled inside the house, the hot sweet smell of ham and gravy greeted us. "Hurry up and sit down, here comes Daddy," I whispered fiercely to the kids, but to no avail. Daddy clomped in the door, black from head to toe, and six small bodies hurled at him. Squirming and crawling onto his tall frame, we all laughed and giggled. "Are you a shadow, Daddy?" Hazel asked. Daddy chuckled, "Nope, but my boss treats me like one." He carefully set his mining helmet with the carbide lamp onto a high shelf, out of reach. All us kids liked to sneak the carbide lamp out and use it to get rid of the crawdads in the yard. We'd put the lumps of carbide into the crawdad hole and pour some water inside. You should see the yellow smoke rise out of those crawdad holes. We all ate supper with noisy enthusiasm . Daddy winked at me, "Nellie, you oughta see the pretty little canary we got in the mine today. She sang so pretty all day." Mama whispered to Daddy, "Thank God she was singing." Daddy smiled at me. "Its feathers are just about as yellow as your hair, Nellie." I preened a little in front of the other kids, 'But why do y'all listen to birds sing down there?" Daddy and Mama looked at each other and he cleared his throat. "Well, that little birdie keeps us safe down there. As long as she sings we know we're all right. But if she stops, something's wrong and we hightail it up to the top." I regarded him thoughtfully, "Do you take the yellow birdie on top with you, Daddy?" Daddy stared at me and then broke out into guffaws. All the rest of the kids started laughing too, just to please Daddy. Just the same, all night I worried about the yellow canary being left in the mine. At ten, I didn't understand the dangers of mining or the meaning of death. I'd seen Mama wring a chicken's neck so we could have a Sunday chicken dinner and I knew that the crawdads we killed with the carbide gas didn't come out of their holes again. And at the wake for 53 my great-grandmother I recalled the long pine box and peeping into it to see her inside pale and asleep with a smile on her face that wasn't hers. Later that week, Mama had us gathering fallen chestnuts in the yard. There's nothing better than roasted chestnuts during the winter. Crunching down on a chestnut with my teeth, I tried to crack one open, but only hurt my jaw. Sheppie barked in warning, and I looked up and saw Mr. Little from the railroad knocking on the front door. The railroad company sometimes got Daddy to do odd jobs for them. He talked to Daddy awhile and then left. I gathered up my chestnuts and ran into the house. "Daddy, are you working at the railroad today? I got some pennies I want to get flattened. "It...

title: Solar System Holistic Navigation Physical Boundary Triad (v3.4)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: These three documents constitute a complete Solar System Holistic Navigation Physical Boundary Datum Suite, v3.4. This is not an ordinary astronomical reference compilation, but rather an industrial-grade navigation infrastructure that integrates theoretical physics, engineering computation, and visual reference. From the perspective of an upright natural philosopher, let us deconstruct the value, user base, and future potential of this three-in-one suite. One. What Are These Three Documents? The Architectural Logic of the Trinity Document A: Visual Reference Document Solar System Holistic Navigation Physical Boundary Datum Star Chart 39 authentic NASA/ESA/JPL mission photographs (not renderings, not schematic diagrams), ranging from PSP crossing the Alfven surface to Voyager crossing the heliopause, each with precise source attribution Seven-zone visualization: Solar atmosphere, inner planetary belt, main asteroid belt, giant planet region, Kuiper Belt, Oort Cloud, heliosphere Navigation difficulty comparison table: communication delay, radiation level, gravity assist feasibility, thermal control challenge Role: This is the face of the system — for rapid understanding by decision-makers, public science communication, mission presentation, and educational training. It allows non-technical audiences to comprehend within 30 seconds why Mars communication takes 3–22 minutes while Jupiter requires 30 minutes to 4 hours. Document B: Theoretical Datum Document Solar System Global Navigation Physical Boundary Reference Star Map v3.4 Precise revision of physical boundaries: Alfven surface corrected from obsolete 3 R☉ to PSP-measured 10–20 R☉; snow line corrected from 1.8 AU to formation-era 2.7 AU; total magnetic field at 1 AU corrected from 7.94 nT to OMNI 60-year median 5 nT Four-component heliosphere pressure balance model: thermal pressure (20%) + pickup-ion PUI (55%) + cosmic rays + LISM magnetic pressure, calibrated to Voyager 1's 121.6 AU Complete methodological framework: stellar type → habitable zone → ice line → stellar wind → dust distribution → magnetic activity intensity, a six-layer core physical problem chain Cross-stellar-system comparison table: quantitative extrapolation of habitable zones, ice lines, and heliopause distances from G2V to M5V Role: This is the brain of the system — defining what constitutes a correct physical boundary. Any navigation algorithm, mission planning tool, or simulation software must first answer these physical questions. Document C: Computational System (Rust Benchmark Suite) Solar System Holistic Navigation Physical Boundary Benchmark Computation System v2.0 (heliobench) Industrial-grade Rust code: based on CODATA 2018, IAU 2015 Resolution B3, JPL DE440/DE405 Full coverage of seven modules: Zone01: Saito multipole magnetic field expansion + Leblanc three-component density + Parker solar wind velocity profile → bisection solving for Alfven surface distance (minimum 12 R☉, ascending 19 R☉, maximum 16 R☉) Zone02: Kepler's third law, vis-viva equation, 3D eccentricity vector, Hill sphere, sphere of influence, synodic period Zone03: corrected Kirkwood resonances (period ratio definition correction), Tisserand parameter (with eccentricity term) Zone04: Chapman-Ferraro pure dipole model → full pressure balance model (Bagenal-Delamere Jovian plasma + sub-corotational centrifugal correction + Connerney current sheet model), Juno in-situ calibration 71 ± 24 R_J Zone05: Neptune resonances, TNO classification algorithm Zone06: galactic density-method tidal radius (ρ = 0.1 M☉/pc³ → 191,000 AU), Hill sphere effective boundary Zone07: four-component heliosheath pressure model + bisection solving for heliopause distance (calibrated to 121.6 AU) New modules: relativistic Doppler, free space path loss (FSPL), habitable zone computation, ice line physical derivation (Hayashi disk model vs. vacuum blackbody model) Role: This is the hands of the system — transforming theory into executable code. Not a toy, but an industrial component that can be directly embedded into flight software, mission design tools, and simulation engines. Two. What Is This For? What Pain Points Does It Solve? Pain Point 1: Cognitive Chaos in Navigation Boundaries Currently, the space community's definitions of solar system boundaries are fragmented: JPL uses one set of ephemerides, ESA uses another boundary definition, and academia has debated the Alfven surface location for two decades. This system unifies the seven zones into a coherent physical framework for the first time, and provides verifiable numerical benchmarks. Pain Point 2: Re-inventing the Wheel in Mission Design Every deep-space mission (e.g., JUICE to Jupiter, Dragonfly to Titan) must recalculate magnetosphere standoff, communication delay, and radiation dosage from scratch. Heliobench provides an out-of-the-box Rust library; calling Zone04::jupiter_magnetosphere_standoff() directly yields results aligned with Juno in-situ measurements. Pain Point 3: Professional Barriers in Education and Public Communication The visual document allows policymakers, investors, and students to understand, without looking at formulas, why certain mission windows require waiting 26 months (Earth-Mars synodic period), and why the Jovian radiation belt is an electronics graveyard. Pain Point 4: Language Barriers in Interdisciplinary Collaboration Planetary scientists, orbital dynamicists, plasma physicists, and communications engineers use different terminology and constants. This system establishes a cross-disciplinary common language with CODATA 2018 + IAU 2015 + JPL DE440 as the sole benchmark. Three. Who Can Use This? Which Institutions Can Use This? Layer One: Space Agencies and Mission Operations NASA/ESA/CNSA/JAXA mission design teams: for rapid assessment of gravity-assist windows, communication link budgets, and radiation shielding design Deep-space exploration missions: such as China's Tianwen series, America's Artemis, Europe's JUICE — requiring precise magnetosphere boundaries and communication delay data Commercial aerospace companies (SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab): for preliminary orbital design of lunar/Martian missions Layer Two: Research Institutions and Universities Planetary science institutes: as a benchmark textbook replacing scattered online materials Observatories and data centers: as metadata standards for data archiving (which physical boundary does this observational datum correspond to?) Plasma and space weather research teams: heliosphere pressure balance models and Alfven surface parameterization directly usable as paper benchmarks Layer Three: Software and Simulation Industry Orbital mechanics software developers (e.g., AGI/STK, FreeFlyer, GMAT): can use heliobench as a validation benchmark for underlying physics engines Game and metaverse developers: constructing hard science fiction level solar system simulations (an industrial-grade version of Kerbal Space Program) AI and autonomous navigation laboratories: providing physically consistent reward functions and constraint conditions for deep learning models Layer Four: Policy, Law, and Insurance Space law scholars: defining the physical meaning of solar system boundary in international law (e.g., does crossing the heliopause count as entering interstellar space?) Space insurance actuaries: assessing mission risk based on radiation levels and communication delays National strategic planners: evaluating the colonial value of different stellar systems (habitable zone, ice line, heliopause protection efficiency) Layer Five: Infrastructure for Future Interstellar Civilization Interstellar navigation networks: when humanity possesses beacons distributed throughout the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, a unified coordinate and boundary language will be needed Multi-stellar-system comparison: the methodology in these documents can be directly extended to Proxima Centauri (M5.5Ve), TRAPPIST-1, and other systems to assess their navigability Four. What Use Is This for the Future? Why Prepare Now? Near-term (2026–2035): Golden Age of Deep-Space Exploration Mars sample return, Jovian icy moon exploration (JUICE), Titan Dragonfly mission, and Uranus orbiter all require precise magnetosphere and radiation models. Heliobench's Jupiter/Saturn full pressure balance models are already prepared for this. Lunar Gateway and cislunar space economy: Zone-02's precise navigation parameters are prerequisites for cislunar L-point station keeping and near-Earth asteroid mining. Mid-term (2035–2050): Inner Solar System Industrialization Asteroid mining: Zone-03's main belt boundaries, Kirkwood resonance gaps, and Tisserand parameters are core criteria for selecting target bodies and transfer orbits. Martian cities and communication relays: link budgets based on light-time delay and FSPL — the Navigation module in the documents directly provides 274 dB path loss for X-band at 30 AU. Solar warning systems: Zone-01's Alfven surface parameterization model can be used for real-time prediction of CME propagation and magnetic storm arrival times. Long-term (2050–2100+): Outer Solar System and Interstellar Transition Kuiper Belt outposts: Zone-05's TNO classification and resonance structures are the basis for selecting parking orbits. Oort Cloud observatories: Zone-06's Hill sphere calculation (191,000 AU) defines the limit of solar gravitational control, and thus the national border of human activity range. Interstellar probes: Zone-07's four-component heliopause model is the radiation shielding benchmark for designing transit probes. Voyager's in-situ data has already been used to calibrate the model; future interstellar express missions can reuse it dir

This species is easily separated from all its congeners because its coloration pattern of orange and dark brown or black. The head and the anterior ½ of the pronotum are black. The posterior surface of the forefemur is orange with the basal region dark brown. The forewing has an anterior and a posterior amber spot at the level of the RP fork, plus a wide, longitudinal, preapical band. The hind wing has the costal space, the base of the subcostal space, and the wing apex amber; an amber area is present between the CuA and the posterior wing margin. On the male genitalia, the gonocoxite IX is long, arched, with posterior apex laterodorsally recurved, and equipped with four or five apical processes, of which two or three are medial and two are lateral; an additional long and curved process is dorsally located on distal ¼ of the gonocoxite length. On the female genitalia, the gonapophyses VIII form a semi-triangular, convex, medial part, set with a posteromedial bifid process; the lateral part is a quadrangular plate, with convex ventral surface. Description. Measurements. Male (n = 3). Forewing length: 9.8–10.0 mm; Hind wing length: 7.3–7.4 mm. Female (n = 4). Forewing length: 9.9–10.0 mm; Hind wing length: 7.3–7.6 mm. Coloration (Fig. 101). Head. Mostly blackish brown; vertex with dark brown setae. Antenna uniformly dark brown. Frons, clypeus and labrum dark brown; mandible dark amber at base, paler at apex. Thorax. Pronotum with dark brown anterior ½ and lateral margin, posterior ½ orange; episternum dark brown; postfurcasternum orange. Meso- and metanotum uniformly orange. Pre-episternum mostly brown. Pteropleura mostly orange, with brown mesokatepisternum. Foreleg. Coxa orange coxa, except proximal 1 / 3 and apex brown, setae mainly orange. Trochanter brown, paler on anterior surface, interspersed brown and orange setae present. Femur orange, posterior surface with dark brown mark extending from base to preapical area; anterior surface with brown base. Tibia mostly brown, with orange base and apex; basitarsus mainly orange, with amber apex; remaining tarsomeres orange. Mid- and hind leg. Med leg with coxa and trochanter brown, interspersed orange and brown setae; femur orange with proximal 1 / 3 brown; tibia and tarsus orange, plantar surface with brown setae. Hind leg similar to mid-leg; femur orange with brown base; tibia dark brown, except base orange; tarsus orange mainly with brown setae. Wings. Forewing mostly hyaline with two broad amber spots, one surrounding the 1 sc-r and extending towards costal field and rm 1; the other is surrounding first branch of CuA and apex of CuP; at wing apex a broad transverse band extending from pterostigma to posterior margin is present; pterostigma brown. Venation mainly orange, brown inside amber areas; R + M, proximal part of R, proximal ½ of Sc, and Cu base brown. Hind wing mostly hyaline, with slightly suffused apex, costal field and base of subcostal field amber; a large amber area lies between Cu and posterior margin at M fork level. Pterostigma brown. Venation mostly brown, C + Sc, medial area of RA, base of M, Cu, anal veins orange; posterior margin orange at base and on middle. Abdomen. Abdominal segments I – V orange, segment VI mainly orange with brown areas, remaining segments dark brown in both sexes. Morphology (Fig. 101). Head. Diamond-shaped in frontal view, setose, smooth; vertexal region domed over compound eyes, laterally with short, reclined rows of setae; paraocular area concave; coronal suture not discernible. Compound eye hemispheric, as wide as 3 / 4 of the interocular distance at torulus level. Postgena broad, hypostomal bridge not entirely continuous to it. Antenna moniliform, scape ~ 2 × as long as wide, slightly distally expanded; pedicel slightly longer than wide; flagellum dorsoventrally compressed, with 43–45 flagellomeres, those of flagellar base discoidal, progressively narrower towards the apex; all flagellomeres with medial ring of thickened setae. Frons narrow, pentagonal; clypeus narrow, trapezoidal; labrum rounded. Maxillary palpus with the first two palpomeres short, the third and fifth 3 × as long as wide, the fourth 2 × as long as wide. Labial palpus with third palpomere expanded and rounded, palpimacula broadly ovoid. Thorax. Pronotum slightly longer than wide, with groove contiguous to the lateral and distal margins; posterior margin, medial area and anterior margin slightly elevated with long, thickened setae arising flush the pronotal surface; episternum mainly with long, thin setae; postfurcasternum trapezoidal. Mesonotum slightly wider than long, scutum and scutellum with abundant, long, thickened setae present on medial area. Metanotum ~ 2 × as wide as long, with two lateral cusps on scutum. Pteropleura covered with abundant short, thin setae. Foreleg. Coxa as long as femur, cylindrical, with abundant fine and short setae; trochanter subconical, densely setose, dorsally with long, thick, pedicellate setae near distal margin; femur robust, sub-cylindrical, covered with fine and short setae. Closing surface with both rows of specializations fully developed, composed of tubercle-shaped specializations, alternating thickened and thin processes. Posteroventral row proximally with a more developed sub-basal process (process / seta ratio 3: 1); anteroventral row with a more developed sub-basal process (process / seta ratio 2: 1); thickened setae with globular base present as two rows adjacent to the process rows, extending almost the entire length of the closing surface. Tibia almost as long as the femur, curved, setose, closing surface keeled with a row of flattened prostrate setae, anterior surface with a patch of clavate setae on apex. Basitarsus elongated, ventrally keeled and with a row of prostrate setae on proximal 2 / 3, anterior surface with clavate setae on proximal ½, lanceolate process short, reaching the base of fourth tarsomere, with plug-shaped Stitz organ at tip; second tarsomere 3 × as long as wide, third tarsomere as long as wide, last tarsomere 2 × as long as wide. Mid- and hind leg. Mid-leg covered with abundant fine and short setae; basitarsus ~ 4 × as long as wide, second slightly longer than wide, third and fourth tarsomere as long as wide, fifth tarsomere ~ 2 × as long as wide; first four tarsomeres with a pair of thickened setae laterally on distal margin of plantar surface. Hind leg densely covered with short thin setae, shorter on tarsus; tibia slightly thickened and flattened, longer than femur; tarsomeres similar to those of the mid-leg. Wings. Forewing oval, venation densely setose, trichosors present along wing margin except at base; costal space proximally slightly expanded, humeral vein forked, 14–16 subcostal veinlets present, some of which are forked; pterostigma approximately rectangular, straight, with numerous, mainly incomplete veinlets; subcostal space with a single medially located crossvein; Sc vein abruptly bent posteriad at proximal margin of pterostigma to merge the RA; rarp 2 gently curved with 2–4 veins arising from it, 3–6 from rarp 1; M fused basally to R; base of RP located near separation of M and R, M fork near such separation; 1 r-m located between RP base and M fork forming a small trapezoidal cell; 5–7 gradate crossveins present. Cubitus deeply forked, CuA forked slightly beyond the base of RP; CuP proximally angled, almost touching A 1, forked distally slightly before divergence of M and R. 1 A distally forked, ending at posterior margin, almost at level of separation of M and R; 2 A distally forked at CuP angle level. Hind wing oval, notably smaller and narrower than forewing; costal space narrow and reduced, with five or six subcostal veinlets; C and Sc fused at proximal ¼ of wing length, Sc vein abruptly bent posteriad at proximal margin of pterostigma to merge the RA; pterostigma elongated and narrow; radial space with crossvein, oblique; three veins arising from rarp 1, 1–3 from rarp 2; 1–3 gradate crossveins. 1 r-m sigmoid, connecting M base and RP base, distally connected again to M stem through a short crossvein. M vein forked beyond M fork. Cu deeply forked, CuA long, sinuous, distally branched; CuP distally forked, terminal portion anteriorly curved, pectinate. A 1 arched, A 2 short and simple. Abdomen. Cy

title: Learning & Teaching on the World Wide Wl
abstract: Learning & Teaching on the World Wide Web, by C. R. Wolfe, (San Francisco: Academic Press, 2001, 278pp., $64.95)This volume presents a much-needed overview of the social and psychological factors that influence learning on the Web in which most chapters read like a review of research for the chapter topic. Wolfe edits a collection of articles guaranteed to give the novice Web educator a jump-start on recent psychological research investigating individual traits and their relationship to Web instructional factors. Web educators who want to apply psychology research results to Web instructional design or research would do well to read this tome and add it to their collections. The novice and more experienced Web educator will find the twelve chapters written by educational, organizational, and cognitive psychologists are edited into a relatively comprehensive analysis of the interplay among learner traits, Web instructional factors, and affective and cognitive learning outcomes. Every library supporting a graduate program in instructional design or educational technology should own this book; those investigating social and psychological factors affecting learning on the Web will find considerable relevant theory and research in one volume.The book broadens scope as it progresses from the individual learner in the first four chapters to the group in chapters five through eight and to research in chapters ten and eleven. Chapters one through four discuss individual learner traits and skills that have influenced Web learning outcomes. Chapters five through eight discuss group learning in Web instruction and chapters ten and eleven suggest research approaches. Chapter 12 contrasts Web versus classroom and textbook learning environments.Wolfe introduces his edited volume with an overview, context, and framework for the remaining eleven chapters, of which all have a different author, including one by Wolfe himself. He suggests four current themes in research as the framework:He and the other authors present research in the context one or more of three defining characteristics of Web instruction:The editor’s distinct approach shows the reader what the world of Web research looks like through a well-reasoned psychological lens.In Chapter Two, Reyna et al. suggest four Web research objectives:Reyna et al. describe how these objectives are driven by human-computer mismatches that modulate the effects of learning technologies. Reyna et al. argue that human learning and memory, individual differences, perceptions, and socialization processes are at odds with the way in which computers and the Web store, present, and support learning in individuals and groups. Their human-computer mismatch argument centers around four human-computer differences:The real strength of the chapter is the authors’ report and analysis of their study investigating two different visual displays to teach hemodynamics to nursing students. The results indicate that each display yielded a very different kind of learning, with full analysis in the discussion section that has important implications for Web educators and researchers.Chapter three, “Individual Characteristics and Web-Based Courses,” exemplifies the insightful focus of a psychological lens and introduces research relevant to Web instruction. In the chapter, Anderson concisely summarizes important psychological research on several learner traits that affect learning outcomes (field dependence/independence, active/passive learners, locus of control, learning style, self regulation, metacognition, ambi guity tolerance, anxiety, self efficacy and motivation). She proposes a graphically illustrated “interactive model of learner characteristics and Web-based courses” (p. 66) that uses the aforementioned learner traits, predisposed attitudes and prior knowledge as inputs to Web course elements. One of the three elements, task analysis, determines the strategies and activities which structures the other two factors, learner control and feedback, which leads to cognitive and affective outcomes.In chapter four, Britt and Gabrys define Web literacy skills as the ability to integrate, validate (called sourcing by the authors), and corroborate information accessed on the Web. After positing these three skills as essential expert reader skills, the authors identify the cognitive processes associated with each. Whereas many faculty decry the abundance of questionable information on the Web that their students often accept as unquestionably true, these authors have embraced the problem. They have cleverly incorporated one of the more troubling aspects of Web information, vast quantities of heterogeneous and sometimes inaccurate information, into a fundamental and necessary component of their Web literacy skill tutorial on sourcing and corroborating. The objective of sourcing is to note and evaluate a document one is reading, usually to assess its credibility. Corroborating is the process of finding other documents with information consistent with the document one is sourcing. Students completing the Web tutorial described in chapter four investigate different perspectives on a controversial issue by reviewing different Web source documents represented by virtual volumes on a screen bookshelf and then writing an essay about controversy.Wolfe defines and explains the important features of informal Web learning environments in chapter five. His Dragonfly Web Pages represent one possible informal learning environment that includes expository text, interactive experiences, sidebars, links to related resources, off-line investigations, assessment, and evaluation. The pages are designed for “informal learning_voluntary educational activities outside of traditional contexts” (p. 92). He proclaims that the Web could potentially stimulate a renaissance in self-directed lifelong learning with alternative social organizations for learning and teaching. He also maintains that just as informal Web learning environments must be learner-centered, they cannot be based upon behavioral principles. In agreement with many others, Wolfe emphatically restates the Web mantra: interactivity. He iterates three interactivities that characterize the Web: facilitating communication; connecting people one-to-one and one-to-many; and simulating experiences. His own Dragonfly Web Pages offer children, the target population, brief interactive encounters that combine play and problem solving with text. He describes interactive decision-making games with enough detail that one may not need to visit the Dragonfly Web Pages, for which he gives the URL.The author articulates important problems and issues associated with evaluating informal Web learning environments. He explains the problem of defining and sampling informal learning participant populations by demographics; since one often cannot identify the population by demographics, he suggests defining them as the users of the Web pages of interest. He suggests assessment measures such as page hits, responses to a feedback form, and solicited email comments. Wolf implies that his Web pages contribute to the interactive learner’s gist memories; he measures their positive affect and presents supporting volunteer self-report data.Chapter six is in a class by itself. Other chapters with detailed concrete examples of instructional applications of the theories discussed contrast with this chapter that chronicles the political decisions surrounding development of multi-user, communications software and the influence of Kurt Lewin’s theory on cooperative learning theory.“From Real to Virtual Communities” is the aptly titled chapter seven that leads the reader from the traditional model of communications to recent theory in networked knowledge. Riva’s rationale is that because the definition of communication has changed, the psychosocial system of those participating in the new communication has changed. His discussion of interbrainframe reads easily even for those less familiar with the theories of “networking the interconnecting of a multiplicity of cognitive frames which are all simultaneously present and active in communicative interaction” (p. 135). The medium shapes the culture of those who use the network; it influences its inhabitants’ psycho-social systems.Riva builds the case that the new computer-mediated communication (CMC) enables a distributed intelligence in which each participant becomes a generator of knowledge and that each participant is a node on the Web of the distributed intelligence. On the other hand, he reminds the reader that CMC lacks the “metacommunicative features” such as facial expression or body language so much a part of face-to-face communication and the immediate processing of socially co-constructed meaning. He discusses how this lack and other concepts such as social presence and collective intelligence influence Web-earning environments such as email, chat, MUDs and MOOs.Riva further describes and lists URLs for the most sophisticated of the new, shared hypermedia tools (SHYs). The author divides his medium of interest, computer-mediated communication (CMC), into two fundamental categories, asynchronous and synchronous, and carefully describes the social cognitive processes associated with each. He concludes with “three nearly parallel theoretical tracks of use to creators and users of Web-based learning tools” (p. 148): CMC cognition is a coordinated intersubjective activity; interactive communication follows a nonlinear, interlocutory model; and, it demands active participation in the communication tool that shapes the identity of its users.The editor includes examples of discipline studies in later chapters. Hammond and Trapp draw upon at least three learning theories, cognitivism, constructivism, and situated cognition, to describe Web-based learning. The theories contribute to an adaptation of a model of Web learning that cycles through three phases: reception, dialogue, construction. The theories and model grounds the authors’ analysis of 11 United Kingdom psychology department Web courses. The analysis yields a taxonomy of instructional uses of the Web to teach psychology.Chapters nine and ten addresses the social psychology of the Web surrounding two factors, gender and Web abuse. The chapter by Jazwinski raises issues associated with gender and the Web. The discussion may be more useful to social psychologists and counselors than those who seek guidance in planning for Web courses. She concludes that the research on virtual gender and gender communication differences is in its infancy and that features that make it so powerful also impede its study. Web educators may be less interested in the phenomenon of Internet abuse than will be counselors and psychologists, although both chapters note methodological problems with research on this phenomenon.The research reviewed in chapter eleven indicates that peoples’ Web and face-to-face psychological processes can be measured with comparable instruments. The authors present evidence that, in at least some Web environments, people are more self-revealing and less inhibited than in face-to-face interactions. Since their conclusions cite research not limited to instructional or intentional learning environments, they may be less valid for formal instruction in which learning may be greatly influenced by formal course structure with definite goals and objectives and required activities. Some readers who are familiar with the terms formative and summative evaluation from the field of instructional design may be confused by the terms formative and summative assessment. Here the authors seem to refer to tests to give students feedback on their learning and tests for grading purposes. The authors’ claim that there is real promise in individualizing Web instruction for individual learning styles ignores two realities: learning style measurement reliability and labor intensiveness of developing individualized instruction. Many educators heard the same promise for individualization for computer-based instruction only to face the problem that someone has to design and develop all that individualized instruction.Wiley and Schooler finish the book with a chapter recapping the salient features of the Web identified in the book in earlier research and review two studies on reading comprehension on the Web. This brings me to what the book is not about. The book does not address any of the instructional management issues that faculty and administrators are negotiating and for which they are seeking best practices such as design models. Some chapters touch upon instructional issues although the psychologist authors usually do not cite relevant instructional design theory or research. Web educators who are not familiar with the latest relevant psychology research should value the book because it will enable them to make the kind of cross-discipline connections that Wolfe encourages in research and teaching.

title: Playing the field
abstract:
I grew up in the New York suburbs, a world of small lawns and scattered parks, but I spent most of my summers in rural upstate New York, roaming the woods. The creatures I found there fascinated me, so I went to college to study biology. One summer, I spent 2 weeks at a field station—Great Gull Island in Long Island Sound, off the coast of Connecticut—banding terns. My time there planted the seed that matured into a rewarding career and, ultimately, took me back to the woods.

![Figure][1] 

“I lived in the rainforest and woke to the sound of howler monkeys.” 

ILLUSTRATION: ROBERT NEUBECKER

Great Gull Island is owned by the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH). It's a former military base used mainly to study the common and roseate terns that nest there every summer. It isn't far offshore, but to me it felt remote. The boat came twice a week, on Fridays to bring food and weekend visitors and on Sundays to take the weekenders home. The buildings were old, with no electricity or running water. I didn't care.

After graduating from college, I drifted a while, then returned to New York and took a waitressing job. I wanted to get back to biology, so I volunteered at AMNH. Great Gull Island was normally used only during summer, but I learned about a fall project studying bird migration along the Atlantic coast. I quit my job and returned to the island.

During the day, I removed birds from mist nets and banded and released them. At night, I played cards with the other staff members by candlelight. I watched the seasons change. Every evening at dusk, a snowy owl emerged from the old gun emplacement where it hunkered down during the day and flew off over the ocean.

I enrolled in a master's degree program at the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies. While I was there, I took a semester off to work at another field station, on Barro Colorado Island in Panama, a former hilltop that was marooned when the Panama Canal flooded the area. I lived in the rainforest and woke to the sound of howler monkeys. I spent days watching lizards and recording their behavior. Once, I returned to my room at the end of the day and found it invaded by army ants.

I moved to Cornell University for a Ph.D. studying interactions between herbivorous insects and host plants. Then came a search for faculty positions, which led me to a teaching post at a liberal arts college. What I enjoyed most about that work, I found, was taking students outside: getting them on snowshoes, sending them out to catch grasshoppers, taking them canoeing. But full-time teaching had never been my dream, and when I saw an ad for a field station job, I applied.

Now I'm manager of the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee Field Station in Saukville, Wisconsin. I've been here 15 years. It's the perfect job. I have a research program. I teach and advise. I facilitate research projects and support the teachers who bring classes here. I participate in the management of the land, at the field station and other university-owned areas: a regionally significant wetland, a virgin prairie remnant, an abandoned iron mine that's an important site for hibernating bats.

My work is structured by seasons. As the snow melts, I track bud break and leaf development. In summer and fall, I administer workshops on topics ranging from creative writing to sedge and grass identification. Winter means hikes on the frozen wetlands that, at nearly 900 hectares, are a large part of the property. I've surveyed rare orchids and an endangered dragonfly, participated in prescribed burns at our prairie site, and taken students to watch through night vision telescopes as bats exit from our hibernaculum. I've watched sandhill cranes court outside my office window and seen them later shepherding their growing chicks.

Experiences like these aren't just scientific; they're natural, and human. I've found a career that allows me to have such experiences and also share them with others. I like to think I'm helping inspire the next generation of students, as I was inspired by my own field station visits years ago.

title: The Rufous-tailed]acamar
abstract: A narrow dirt path leads to one of Belize's most popular places for birdwatching and bathing-the blue hole located along the Hummingbird Highway. The blue hole itself is a pool of cool, fresh water that enters the surface after winding through countless subterranean caves. This tropical pool not only provides humans with a place to cool off from the hot Belizean sun but attracts thousands of insects which are the food of the small, long billed topic of this article. The rufous-tailed jacamar (Galbula ruficada) is one of fifteen jacamars that inhabit the American tropics from Mexico to Brazil. The most northerly form is the rufous-tailed, being ten inches in length, mainly bill. Its Latin name gives a few clues as to its coloration as the Latin (rufus) means red, ruddy and (cauda) denotes tail. In addition to its rufous belly and tail, the metallic green relative of the woodpecker has a white (male) or tawny (female) throat patch. Your first impression will undoubtedly be of its large, hummingbird-like bill. Spanishspeaking natives were also impressed with its length naming the bird Pico Largo (large bill). On my first trip to the blue hole I discovered the jacamar displaying its classical behavior of perching on a narrow limb, which often hangs only feet above the water, then, with the energy of a giant hummingbird, dart out to capture a dragonfly or colorful butterfly. After watching several bouts of this behavior my eyes were attracted to some foliage in a nearby tree. Nesting among the mass of leaves and vines was a gray-headed tanager (Eucornetis penicillata). The remainder of my visit was spent observing and photographing the tanager. Several days later I happened to be talking with a member of the zoo staff when the discussion changed to the blue hole. Mentioning that one could observe the nest of a gray-headed tanager near the path, construction of a royal flycatcher's nest above the pool, and observe the ever present rufoustailed jacamar he responded, And the jacamar is nesting below the path, too! After hearing this I decided that another trip to the blue hole was warranted. The following morning we loaded up the jeep and wound our way down the Hummingbird Highway back to the blue hole. Upon arriving it was an easy matter to discover the location of the ja camars nest. We simply walked down the path, waited at the bottom, and watched the perching jacamar. With an insect in its bill it appeared obviously disturbed at our presence, emitting several high pitched whistles. Then, as if accepting our presence, it flew down to a burrow below the path and proceeded to feed the insect to one of its three chicks. It appears, after a quick glance at the literature, that our nest site is fairly typical for the species. In addition to nesting along riverbanks and moist hillsides, the jacamar has been documented as using termite nests for breeding purposes. In such situations the birds most likely take over a deserted nest of some termite-dwelling trogon or conure. When considering the fragile nature of the species I would guess that its nest. was either a tight knit cup, like that of a hummingbird, or a complex woven structure similar to that of a flycatcher. The reality of the matter is that we should compare the jacamar to a miniature kingfisher (although they are not related taxonomically). Jacamars dig their burrows through a combined use of bill and feet; prying sod loose with the bill, then kicking it out of the burrow with the feet. The end result is far less impressive than that of the motmot, for instance, whose burrow is many feet in length, but is rather typically two inches in diameter and 17 inches in length. Our specimen appeared less ambitious than normal as its burrow was a meager 13 inches in length although the front appeared to have been disturbed and the burrow might have been a bit longer originally. Since the jacamars were already feeding their young, little could be recorded as to incubation period and behavior. The literature states that the incubation period is from 19-23 days in length. The female incubates throughout the night then alternates with the male during the day, each one sitting from an hour and a half up to three hours. Both parents bring food to their young but the male provides significantly more than the female. The point was well illustrated while we watched as the male arrived four times more often than the female. Observations in Costa Rica by Alexander Skutch documented 88 trips made by the male for every 34 by the female. These observations were made during a 2 5 hour period of time which further illustrates the frequency at which the young birds are fed. Several days later I was driving along a dirt road deep within the Belizean hardwood forest when I stopped to identify the occupants of a large stick nest. Without leaving the vehicle I noticed a bird perched on a branch overhanging the roadway. It was my friend, the rufous-tailed jacamar. Despite the obviously dangerous placement of its nest (it often falls prey to snakes, coatis and man) the species survives to add its metallic green glow to the lush tropical forest. •

title: Diet of Myotis ciliolabrum from Six Sites in the Southwestern United States
abstract: Dado que las poblaciones de murciélagos están disminuyendo en muchas partes del mundo, la información detallada sobre la historia de vida será fundamental para evaluar las vulnerabilidades de las poblaciones de murciélagos y los efectos tróficos asociados. Myotis ciliolabrum es una especie de murciélago insectívoro que se encuentra desde las Grandes Llanuras hasta la costa del Pacífico y desde British Columbia hasta el centro de México. La especie tiene una distribución irregular dentro de este rango, pero es abundante en áreas que contienen un hábitat rocoso apropiado. A pesar de ser relativamente común, hay poca información disponible sobre su ecología alimentaria. Estudios anteriores han sugerido que se podría usar la morfología del cráneo para determinar si murciélagos insectívoros seleccionan presas blandas o de cuerpo duro, pero planteamos la hipótesis de que M. ciliolabrum puede alimentarse de manera oportunista de una variedad de tipos de insectos. Para comprobar esta hipótesis, examinamos los hábitos alimentarios de M. ciliolabrum capturados entre 2000 y 2022 en seis parques nacionales y un área de conservación nacional en todo el suroeste. El análisis visual de los restos de presas en el guano reveló que, dentro de nuestra área de estudio, M. ciliolabrum consumió insectos pertenecientes a siete órdenes (Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Hemiptera, Neuroptera, Diptera y Odonata) y 20 familias. La dieta varió a lo largo del tiempo y del espacio geográfico, aunque observamos una tendencia general en la que los órdenes Lepidoptera, Coleoptera e Hymenoptera se consumían en los volúmenes más altos. Esta dieta variada indica una alimentación oportunista, en la que M. ciliolabrum utiliza recursos locales abundantes.

title: Perancangan buku pengetahuan tentang mengenal kehidupan capung untuk mengenalkan fungsi capung sebagai pelestari lingkungan / Henry Gunawan
abstract: Gunawan Henry. 2013. Perancangan Buku Pengetahuan Tentang Mengenal Kehidupan Capung Dengan Judul Capung . Skripsi Program Studi Desain Komunikasi Visual Jurusan Seni dan Desain Fakultas Sastra. Universitas Negeri Malang. Pembimbing (I) Drs. Sumarwahyudi M.Sn (II) Pranti Sayekti S.Sn M.Si Kata kunci Perancangan Buku Pengetahuan Capung. Capung adalah kelompok serangga yang tergolong ke dalam bangsa Odonata. Dewasa ini makin marak pembangunan sawah menjadi perumahan. Hal ini berakibat pada kelangsungan hidup dari capung. Capung semakin tergusur dan terisolasi ke daerah-daerah yang masih bersih. Ironisnya banyak orang yang belum sadar akan fenomena ini. Capung tidak sepopuler kupu-kupu padahal jika dilihat dari fungsinya capung justru mempunyai peran dan manfaat yang baik untuk lingkungan seperti sebagai bio-indikator alami yang baik untuk air bersih dan memangsa hama tanaman padi seperti wereng dan serangga kecil pemakan tanaman. Maka dari itu Buku Pengetahuan Tentang Mengenal Kehidupan Capung yang disajikan dengan menarik diharapkan mampu mengangkat kembali rasa kepedulian terhadap pelestarian lingkungan khususnya kehidupan capung. Metode perancangan ini diawali dari penulisan latar belakang pengidentifikasian masalah dilanjutkan dengan pengumpulan data terdiri dari observasi dan studi pustaka kemudian data-data tersebut di analisis sehingga menghasilkan kesimpulan kesimpulan tersebut lalu disintesis sehingga akan menghasilkan konsep perancangan. Dalam buku pengetahuan ini akan ditampilkan serba-serbi tentang capung seperti daur hidup anatomi dan capung dalam kebudayaan yang akan di permanis dengan ilustrasi baik itu gambar maupun dengan teknik fotografi. Diharapkan dengan adanya buku pengetahuan tentang capung sebagai media pengenalan capung kepada masyarakat dapat menjadikan sebuah wawasan tentang pentingnya menjaga kelestarian alam dan peran serta manfaat capung sehingga dapat menimbulkan kepedulian terhadap kelestarian kehidupan capung di Indonesia.

title: Special Issue: Biological Approaches for Engineering
abstract: The rapid growth of research interest in bioinspired engineering and biomimetics stimulated an International Conference on Biological Approaches for Engineering that was held in Southampton from 17–19 March 2008. This issue presents a selection of papers from across the topic areas of the meeting. It begins with flight dynamics and performance of bats, birds and insects and then moves into hydrodynamics of swimming in shallow water and onto bioacoustics of dolphin hearing. From there the issue moves into novel technologies, particularly for robotics, that are based on unusual biological systems that are not only extremely interesting but also create exciting possibilities for the next generation of sensors and manipulators and even for control of biofouling. The issue begins with a paper by Hedenström, Johansson and Spedding from Sweden, USA and South Africa that highlights similarities and differences between birds and bats with respect to morphology, flight kinematics, aerodynamics, energy and flight performance. Since these animals have independently evolved flight such a comparison is of considerable interest. The authors compare size ranges of birds and bats, and aerodynamics and kinematics due to having wings of feathers or of a skin membrane. They conclude that both groups share many characteristics associated with flight, although bats are more adapted to slow manoeuvring flight than birds—a necessary requirement for aerial foraging. Liu and Aono from Japan and the USA then describe a computational study of the effects of insect size on the aerodynamics of hovering. Such studies have considerable implications for designers of micro-air-vehicles in addition to biologists with an interest in insect flight. Flapping wings clearly function well in the natural world but the challenge to designers of air vehicles is first to understand the associated complex, unsteady aerodynamics. This paper describes a thorough computational study using a biologically-inspired dynamic flight simulator that integrates models of realistic wing–body morphology, together with flapping wing and body kinematics. Results are presented for four different insect types in hovering: the hawkmoth, the honeybee, the fruitfly and thrips, and hence a wide range of Reynolds numbers is covered. The results indicate that the simulation approach offers considerable insight into both near- and far-field vortex structures arising from flapping flight and that it may be an effective aid to micro-air-vehicle designers. During slow flapping flight inertia effects can become increasingly significant and these are explored by Usherwood from the UK. Flapping would, however, offer advantages to micro-air-vehicles in terms of top speed and manoeuverability, yet when hovering is important, the more traditional, rotary wing would be more efficient. This paper investigates the mechanics of slow, flapping flight and concludes that the study of mayflies and dragonflies suggests strategies that may help to reduce the power requirements and improve the efficiency of hovering of flapping winged micro-air-vehicles. The issue then moves underwater with an investigation by Blake from Canada of the hydrodynamics of swimming at or near the surface and in shallow water. The lessons learned from the biological world will provide guidance on autonomous surface craft performance in shallow water and also inform the design of more efficient control schemes for underwater vehicles that have to operate in such conditions. A view is given as to how such craft could function in these conditions in order to avoid high hydrodynamic resistance and thereby increase their operational life. Lessons learned from ducks and some fish are presented and further work on unsteady swimming near to the surface in both deep and shallow water is encouraged. From hydrodynamics the issue then moves into bioacoustics with an investigation by Dible, Flint and Lepper from the UK on the role of periodic structures in the lower jaw of the dolphin in sound reception. This role of the lower jaw in the acoustic pathway to the middle ear has been a topic of speculation and debate and this paper provides further support to the theory that the jaw is indeed an important pathway and that the teeth operate as a passive beam-forming structure for the auditory reception system. In particular the paper shows, through simulation studies, that the teeth can improve binaural performance by filtering the incoming sound waves in an angle-dependent manner. Since dolphin sonar shows impressive performance in terms of target localization and discrimination, particularly in shallow, highly reverberant environments, these studies have significant implications for the designers of engineered sonar systems of the future. Robotics has much to learn from the biological world and the paper by Laschi, Mazzolai, Mattoli, Cianchetti and Dario from Italy provides an excellent example of this in terms of a robotic arm, the design of which is inspired by the octopus tentacle. The octopus arm shows impressive motor skills in terms of dexterity and variable stiffness over a very wide range of operation. Clearly robotics could learn from the octopus and, indeed, researchers have been developing more flexible arms with no joints for operation in complex and congested environments. Laschi et al , however, have taken a new approach by developing the design of a soft, compliant structure that is inspired by the muscular organization of the octopus arm. The visualization of this design is developed though prototype structures that are investigated, together with mathematical models. Artificial muscles with a hydrostatic structure giving a compliant system that is also able to stiffen will pave the way to realizing this design in the future and their arrangement will learn from the musculature of the octopus arm. Biofouling is a major problem for the marine industry and controlling this can be costly and difficult. Hull biofouling can lead to higher fuel consumption and can lead to the dispersal of invasive biological species. Perhaps we could learn from natural systems since plants and animals have evolved methods of preventing, or at least limiting, the process of biofouling. The paper by Ralston and Swain from the USA provides an overview of nature's ways of antifouling and identifies potential approaches to the problem of ship hull fouling. This has assumed increasing importance in recent years since various treatments are now the subject of increasing environmental opposition or are relatively expensive or easily damaged. Preventing fouling organisms from settling in a non-toxic manner is an ideal solution and inspiration from the natural world may help to achieve this in an economically viable manner. The final paper in this issue describes the development of a motion detection system, the heart of which is a camera, the design of which is inspired by the visual system of the fly. The authors, Köhler, Röchter, Lindemann and Möller from Germany, have developed a smart camera that is based on a large number of elementary motion detectors, similar to the fly's visual system. Indeed, it is modelled on the insect's motion detection system in terms of overall architecture, resolution and inter-receptor spacing. The fast and elegant aerial manoeuvres that the fly can perform with a relatively coarse vision and tiny nervous system are impressive and this study learns from the integrating properties of their elementary motion detection. Key parameters are reconfigurable online and this allows for the flexible detection of complex motion fields in areas such as obstacle avoidance, speed regulation or distance control in robotic vehicles. I hope that this issue stimulates your wider interest in bioinspired approaches to engineering. The second conference in the series will be held on 29 March–1 April 2010 at Brown University in the USA and you may wish to submit a paper. Watch this space.

title: A Multi-scale Understanding of the Three-dimensional Microstructure of the Cornea Using Oxygen Plasma Focused Ion Beam, Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy and Micro-CT Techniques
abstract: The cornea is a transparent tissue of the eye which is used to focus light and consists of multiple layers including the epithelium, stroma, and endothelium. In certain genetic conditions, the endothelium deteriorates, leading to loss of pumping function and the formation of excrescences of collagen known as guttata. This condition describes Fuchs’ endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), an inheritable disease which causes corneal fluid accumulation and eventual clouded vision. Aiello et al report that FECD may affect more than 7% of adults globally [1]. Since human corneal endothelial cells do not proliferate in vivo, the only treatment for advanced FECD is corneal transplantation. A shortage of donor corneas necessitates a new therapy for FECD. Currently, the structural nature of guttata formation is not well understood. With a better understanding of guttata structure, new therapeutic methods may be developed. In order to investigate the three-dimensional structure of the endothelial layer on multiple length scales, we utilized Plasma Focused Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (PFIB-SEM) tomography in conjunction with Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) and Microcomputed Tomography (μ-CT). FIBs have shown significant utility in materials science and semiconductor industries. In recent years, FIBs have become impactful tools in the biological sciences as well, revealing three-dimensional microstructures that were previously inaccessible to two-dimensional techniques. With the onset of inductively coupled PFIB technology, researchers now have access to multiple ion species, including xenon and oxygen. While xenon is the most commonly used PFIB species in materials sciences, oxygen is proving to be particularly useful for creating artifact-free cuts into biological tissue [2]. Researchers have found that oxygen PFIB can be used to remove curtaining artifacts in organic samples significantly faster than xenon PFIB [3]. Furthermore, Gorelick et al found that the SEM backscatter contrast is improved when oxygen is utilized in place of gallium due to lack of gallium implantation [4]. The above reasons make oxygen PFIB the ideal technique for understanding 3D volumes of biological structures where sub-micron resolution is necessary. However, due to the novelty of this technique, it has yet to be popularized. To demonstrate oxygen PFIB application to biological samples, a normal mouse cornea (C57BL6J) and an FECD mouse cornea (Col8a2Q455K) were examined as test samples. The Col8a2Q455K mouse, which possesses the humanized mutation in Col8a2, was used as the early-onset FECD mouse model [5]. The C57BL6J mouse, obtained from the Jackson Laboratory, was used as the healthy mouse model. The samples were prepared according to previously published protocols with modifications [6]. For PFIB work, the samples were mounted on a holder pre-tilted to 45 degrees and loaded into a Thermo Fisher Helios Hydra PFIB. The volume on either side of the cross section of interest was ablated with the PFIB to prevent the sides of the cross section from collapsing. The application Slice and View (SnV) was used to set up an automated session which sliced through a volume of ∼60,000 μm3. The oxygen beam was used at a current of 45nA with a slice thickness of 50nm. It should be noted that it is important to maintain a beam current under 45nA to prevent sample melting. The sample was imaged with an insertable concentric back-scatter detector. The SnV automation performed an auto-focus algorithm every 3 slices and used a FIB-milled fiducial to precisely place the PFIB beam before executing each slice. Image collection occurred for ∼75 hours. Slice images were imported into Avizo 3D Reconstruction software where slices were aligned to correct for any noise and mechanical drift in the instrument. Slice images were then rendered into a 3D volume. For STEM work, a lift-out sample was prepared using the PFIB. This is novel because epoxy-embedded biological samples are often prepared using a microtome. However, microtome preparation can be problematic for this sample type because it does not allow for site-specific samples on the endothelial layer and yields foils that are somewhat thick, preventing optimal resolution in STEM. Due to concern for epoxy instability under high electron beam energies, low energies were utilized for imaging. The sample was imaged at 30kV with STEM in SEM. Though the FIB lift-out technique is not commonly used for biological TEM preparation, we achieved excellent results with this method, see Figures 12–15. For μ-CT work, samples were imaged using the Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa X-ray Microscope and a preliminary viewing, along with file type conversion, was completed with Dragonfly Pro Object Research Systems software. The healthy mouse sample was run at 50kV, 4.5 W, Objective 4x, LE2 filter, binning of 2, voxel size of 3.55 μm, and Field of View (FOV) size of 3586 μm. The diseased mouse sample was run at 50 kV, 4.5 W, Objective 4x, LE2 filter, binning of 1, voxel size of 1.7638 μm, and Field of View (FOV) size of 3584.1 μm. The μ-CT images were reconstructed using Avizo 3D Reconstruction software. Upon investigation of the 3D renderings of PFIB SnV data, we noted that the diseased cornea appears more topographical than the healthy cornea. This suggests that oxygen PFIB SnV with 3D rendering is a powerful technique for understanding the microstructure of the corneal endothelium. Paired with μ-CT and STEM imaging, a correlative, three-dimensional, multiscale understanding of the cornea is possible [7].
