title: China in Twentieth- and Twenty-First-Century African Literature
abstract: In “Another Way in the World,” his introduction to the 2016 PMLA special issue on “Literature in the World,” Simon Gikandi poses the question of what it means to enact an epistemological shift in world and comparative literary studies, one that engages Global South dialogues that are not overdetermined by Western mediation (1203). Duncan Yoon’s outstanding book finds another way, or in the author’s word, the elsewhere in the African literary world, by reading contemporary African texts within the conceptual framework of postcolonial and Africa–China studies. More specifically, Yoon asks: How do contemporary African writers imagine Africa–China relations in ways that challenge the sensational perception of China’s presence in Africa? How does this mode of imagination unsettle the fixation of postcolonial critique in African literary scholarship on Western encounters with Africa, occluding other forms of historical and cultural encounters that shape the African world? China in Twentieth- and Twenty-First-Century African Literature poses these profound questions to initiate conceptual, methodological, and analytical moves that open up an alternative trajectory of postcolonial African literature. Through these critical moves, the book calls for “a radical decentering of the West so that it is no longer the primary point of comparison for postcolonial literature and, by extension, postcolonial identity” (209).Yoon writes this book against the background of the mainstream discourse of political economy and the media that often frames the relationship between Africa and China as another relation of domination, with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) holding economic power and political agency. The book ponders how African literary discourse reimagines this relation in ways that address the messiness of politico-economic realism and shifting historical vision. In this critical direction, Yoon unravels the multiple symbolic dimensions of China in the African literary imagination using the concepts of alluvium (building on Édouard Glissant’s theorization) and durée (following Achille Mbembe) to overturn the dominant concepts of political economic analysis that glosses over complex and heterogeneous cultural formations emerging in “the African experience of China” (3). Used conjunctively, the concept of alluvium unpacks the historical and cultural sedimentations that shape the shifting and entangled realities of political economic configurations, racial formations, and diasporic identities, and the durée lays out the interlocking threads of events integral to these realities (11, 65). If literary engagement with the political economy of Africa–China relations constitutes the book’s major conceptual intervention, another concerns its radical remapping of the geography of postcolonial theory. Focusing on African literary texts published between 1965 and 2019, it shifts the paradigm of postcolonial critique in African literature from engagement with Western colonialism and the trans-Atlantic circuit of globalization to China as an imaginary construct and historical, political, economic, and ideological force. In this way, Yoon’s book reorients postcolonial studies by bringing together global Cold War studies, Global South studies, and Indian Ocean studies with critical attention to the varied forms of African literary and discursive engagement with China.Methodologically, Yoon’s bold approach to African literature deconstructs the dominant paradigm of Africa–Europe relations by taking China as a ground of comparison at the intersecting levels of formal, historical, and geographical worldliness. At the formal level, the book’s critical calibrations of different literary forms incisively elucidate the heterogeneous imaginaries of China in African literature. Its compelling comparative analysis peels the layers of complexity in Africa–China relations as represented in African poetry, novels, and life-writing forms. At the historical level, Yoon performs “chiastic” readings of literary texts and history, which account for the differential repetition and reversive structure of experience, to situate contemporary relations within multiple histories of Afro-Chinese encounters (9): the pre- and early modern Indian Ocean encounter, the Chinese indentured labor migration of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the Afro-Asian solidarity forged during the Cold War and decolonization moments, and the more recent migration of labor, capital, and resources between the PRC and Africa. Through this collision of form and history, other geographies of African literature reveal intricate dynamics of national and transnational exchanges “texturized” (a term Yoon invokes again and again) in the literary representations of China’s relationship with Ghana, Zambia, Cameroon, South Africa, Congo-Brazzaville, and Kenya. In its interdisciplinary engagement with form, space, and time, the book recasts the global geographies and economies of relations and extraction in Afro-Chinese encounters.Moreover, Yoon’s illuminating literary analysis deploys the alluvial as a symbolic thread to tease out the composite layers of historical, economic, cultural, and racial experience shaping China’s encounters with Africa. In the first chapter, Yoon explores Ghana–China relations in Kofi Awoonor’s poetry and life-writing in the context of the Third World solidarity during the Cold War and its aftermath. The chapter offers a forceful reading of China as a contradictory symbol of revolution and its disenchantment and more specifically examines the figuration of Maoism in Awoonor’s geopolitical imagination. As an operating concept, the alluvial functions as a figure of history in Awoonor’s poetic fashioning of indigenous aesthetics in response to the historical imagination of Afro-Asian solidarity. Situating the alluvial in the material dynamics of mineral resource extraction and chauvinistic nationalism, Chapter 2 extends the conversation on Ghana–China relations in a comparative framework with Zambia–China relations. The chapter reads the representation of gold and copper mines as spaces of extraction to address Chinese extractivist practices in the Ghanaian and the Zambian novels, Kwei Quartey’s Gold of Our Fathers (2016) and Mukuka Chipanta’s A Casualty of Power (2016).In the third chapter, the alluvial becomes a figure for reading the complexity of cultural and diasporic identity while challenging racist narratives of anti-Blackness and anti-Chineseness. Precisely, the chapter turns to the question of the Chinese diaspora in South Africa and the African diaspora in China through memoirs written by the South African–born Chinese writer and journalist Ufrieda Ho, Paper Sons and Daughters: Growing Up Chinese in South Africa (2011), and the Cameroonian writer Jean Tardif Lonkog, The Black Man and His Visa (2013). These memoirs explore the precarity of diasporic existence through the representation of risk and dream as constituted in the texts’ gambler/trickster figures. In the fourth chapter, Yoon moves from Anglophone to Francophone Africa to perform an alluvial reading of race and racialization in the context of the Congo–China relations through the prominent Congolese writer, politician, and diplomat Henri Lopès’s novel, Le lys et le flamboyant (1997). The chapter challenges the fiction of absolute racial and national belonging by reading the representation of creolization in the novel’s rearticulation of Afro-Chinese identities.It is crucial to note that Yoon persuasively builds the argument about the discursive circulation of China in African literature on the theoretical claim that the PRC’s presence in Africa cannot be conflated with Western colonialism and neocolonialism. To justify this claim, Yoon makes concerted efforts in Chapter 2 to quantitatively and qualitatively differentiate between Western colonialism and what he designates “Chinese extractivism” based on the unprecedented cultural, political, and economic “scope and scale” of the former (55). He clarifies that even though Chinese extractivism “replicates colonial mechanisms” that recall the traumatic memory of colonial violence (55), it does not fundamentally enact a (neo)colonial relationship with Africa. While it is undebatable that conflating Western colonialism with China’s presence in Africa flattens the complex configurations of geopolitical, historical, and cultural relations, creating an insistent distinction between colonialism and extractivism risks downplaying the global mutations of colonial power that structure multiple forms of extractive forces. Of course, Yoon offers a radical critique of the extractive logics of empire that reproduce planetary and quotidian conditions of unsustainable life. And he is right to contend that: “The PRC may very well stage a new bid for global hegemony by beginning on the African continent, but to assume its inevitability is to ignore African agency (an old colonial trope) and miss the new terms of empire through which this bid is made” (221). Yet the articulation of “the new terms of empire” cannot escape, to adapt Yoon’s methodological language, the chiastic operations of the old and the new. Careful attention to these chiastic operations demands taking the differential parallels and reversive transformations of colonial extractivism as a point of departure.Despite the troubled differentiation of the colonial from the extractive, Yoon’s book poses a significant challenge to the populist instrumentalization of discursive orthodoxies through which Africa–China relations are often (mis)understood. It calls for the critical need to understand the present geopolitical relationship within the context of the long history of Afro-Chinese encounters. This deep historicization of geopolitical relations is a necessary epistemic measure required to unsettle the ahistorical understanding of racial and cultural identity on the one hand and globalization and empire on the other. Yoon’s conclusion bolsters this overarching critical insight through a perceptive reading of Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor’s 2019 novel, The Dragonfly Sea, which stages the drama of alluvial consciousness in the Indian Ocean imaginaries of the Kenya–China historical and cultural relation. In the context of the present geopolitical and economic anxieties about China’s presence in Africa, Yoon’s book shows how African writers not only interrogate these anxieties in their literary engagement with history, political economy, and culture, but also provide textured imaginative portraits of Afro-Chinese relations.

title: Collecting Trips and Bugsters
abstract: John Acorn lectures at the University of Alberta. He is an entomologist, broadcaster, and writer, and is the author of 15 books, as well as the host of two television series. How many of you go on “collecting trips”? The expression has ben a part of the entomological lexicon for a very long time, and I have been using it since grade school, when I began collecting insects. I suspect, though, that I called such events “going bug catching” before I clued in to the fact that “collecting trip” was the preferred phrase. Over the years, however, I have noticed fewer and fewer people saying “collecting trip,” to the point where it has started to catch my attention each time I hear it. After all, there is something a bit dated about the expression, but it is not immediately apparent to me where the anachronism lies. Perhaps it deserves a closer look. Of course, collecting trips are, quite literally, trips on which one collects something, which, for entomologists, usually means insect specimens. Collecting trips are specimen acquisition trips. Most of the time, these specimens come back freshly killed, but I doubt that anyone chooses a different term for the outing when the objective is to “bring ‘em back alive” (another anachronistic phrase, associated with large animal collector Frank Buck, who used it as his personal signature line, back in the 1930s). In fact, I have been on many collecting trips during which not a single specimen was collected, and I have noticed that for some entomologists, “collecting trip” is more or less synonymous with “going outside.” I suspect that for many entomologists whose work takes place in a lab or a greenhouse, the only time they had to go outside to do entomology was the time they made a collection for a taxonomy course. A bugster on a collecting trip, or a biologist who has gone out? Either way, it's Heather Proctor, looking for water mites in a shallow lake in Alberta. “Field trip” is an obvious alternative to “collecting trip,” especially when the objective is to observe, photograph, or measure, or do any of the sorts of things that are typical in applied entomology, ecology, or behavioral studies. Collecting is usually associated with taxonomists, while other sorts of ecologists prefer to “sample,” even when it means exactly the same thing. So many people use the generic term “field trip” to describe an entomological outing, or the term “field work,” which has the advantage of sounding more rigorous, and avoiding the impression that one has gotten away with something by getting out of the office, which, for many entomologists, is strangely called “the lab.” “Field trip” has a Wikipedia entry. There, it is explained that field trips are usually educational in nature, but that “much of the early research into the natural sciences was of this form.” Not only that, “Charles Darwin is an important example of someone who has contributed to science through the use of field trips.” Well, yes, obviously. The Field Trip of the Beagle would have been an amusing book title, I'll admit, but The Collecting Trip of the Beagle would not have been too far off the mark. Even hardcore taxonomists realize that they are collecting more than specimens when they are “in the field,” and that they are also accumulating experience with their study organisms in nature and formulating ideas about habitats, interactions, and other aspects of ecology and evolution, just like Darwin. A quick Google search for the term “collecting trip” shows that those who do such things, other than entomologists, are generally looking for fossils, minerals, shells, plants, live tropical fish, herpetiles, or ethnographic materials such as songs or stories. But what other terms might we use? “Entomological outing” might seem appropriate, but it sounds a bit wishy-washy, since “outing” has a social feel to it, along with “stepping out,” or “going out on the town.” “Expedition” is too formal, and these days it echoes the marketing language of outdoor clothing manufacturers, and therefore sounds a bit cheesy. Ornithologists often call their activities “birding,” and herpetologists go “herping,” but the verbification of “insect” to “insecting” has never, to my knowledge, been attempted. “Bugging,” on the other hand, does have its proponents, and I have contributed to this line of thinking with the phrase “night bugging,” which was also the title of a song, in the night-bugging episode of my former television show, Acorn, the Nature Nut . Most night bugging, however, is referred to as “light trapping,” “blacklighting,” or “night collecting.” Some butterfly-watching enthusiasts use the word “butterflying,” but I must admit I have not heard this expression from the mouth of an actual lepidopterist. “Mothing” is more common, and “beetling” is common too. I haven't heard “dragonflying,” but I have heard “odeing” (or is that “oding”?). I suspect that specialists on particular groups of insects have their own colloquial terms for the pursuit of their subjects in the field. Aquatic entomologists, or at least those who work in ponds, go “pond dipping,” while a variety of other entomologists participate in “sweep netting,” “splashing,” “rock flipping,” “bark peeling,” and a variety of other specialized activities. The term “botanizing,” on the other hand, only rarely has an equivalent in “entomologizing.” Even the term “entomologist” has its challenges. For some people, there is a perceived conflict between being an entomologist, and therefore being interested in insects, and being something “broader” such as an evolutionary biologist or an ecologist. Personally, I think anyone who studies insects and avoids the word “entomologist” has failed a sort of personality test. I feel confident diagnosing them with a form of intellectual snobbery, and I hope they get better soon. Perhaps the use of “collecting trip” is part of what identifies us as entomologists, such that anyone who works with insects and says “collecting trip” would probably identify themselves as an entomologist. (Perhaps I should say “self-identify,” but I don't identify myself as the sort of person who uses “self-identify,” so I avoid that phrase.) There are, however, few useable synonyms for “entomologist,” and that is a shame. Ornithologists can call themselves “birders,” but entomologists can't quite get away with “insecter,” or even “hexapoder.” Neither word is even close to euphonious. “Bugger” is out, for obvious reasons, although “bugging trip” seems to avoid any unwanted associations with the word “bugger.” The word “bugster” is a good alternative, and I find that at least some amateur entomologists are beginning to adopt it for themselves. My license plate reads “BUGSTER” (my wife got it for me on my birthday many years ago), and I find that it helps explain what I am doing, parked along some country road, with a net in my hand, prowling the roadsides. Perhaps the nub of it all is that collecting implies specimens, and specimens are real objects. Those who wish to give the impression that they care more about ideas, abstractions, and processes do everything they can to avoid the impression that they are interested in real objects, despite the fact that “objects” are both complicated and the very basis of the world in which we live. This is, of course, my way of returning to the familiar challenge of justifying natural history in today's scientific environment. Not that biologists are the only people out of touch with real objects. I was chatting with my son Jesse this morning about his experiences as a second-year electrical engineering student. He has been learning about designing electrical circuits, but always as simulations, never as real components with real wires and real current passing through it all. Since he builds such things at home all the time, the simulations seem a bit silly to him. He also told me a story about the electrical engineering student club. In their tiny clubhouse office, they have an old component stereo that wasn't working. They thought perhaps Jesse could fix it, since he was the only person in the group who knows how to solder. The other students had many theories about why the stereo was silent, ranging from old capacitors to broken solder joints. When Jesse had a look, it turned out that these engineers-in-training had failed to insert one of the speaker wires into its connector. The parallels to natural history are obvious, and a second event this morning also caught my eye. A Dutch friend on Face-book posted a link to a recent paper on the need for better natural history training in the environmental sciences in general ( Barrows et al. 2016 ), and a Spanish friend of his immediately responded, “we used to call it going out.” The article is worth a look. I was especially interested in the suggestion that a major aspect of scientific natural history involves citizen science projects, which made me wonder: what do citizen scientists call it when they go outside to do the things they do? “Citizen sciencing”? I doubt it. Perhaps there is no single best term for engaging with insects outdoors, but after exploring the subject here, I am personally happy to advocate a healthy sort of pluralism. Let's use whatever term seems to fit the moment, but please, let's also keep the traditions alive, and go on “collecting trips” from time to time, even if all we collect are memories and photographs.

title: Revolutionizing Dementia Care
abstract: Video: Revolutionizing Dementia Care (59 min) Senior Producer and Director: Mason Mills Release Date: 2018 Available:https://ideastations.org/RevolutionizingDementiaCare or https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=revolutionizing+dementia+care+documentary Gerontologists are becoming increasingly aware of the advent and growth of the person-oriented model of care for individuals diagnosed with dementia or related conditions. Our On Film and Digital Media team has shared previous reviews of wonderful documentaries illustrating individually tailored applications of such care as creative role involvement, personalized music, and painting (Scheidt, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2019, respectively). I know some gerontologists who believe that the person-oriented paradigm will ultimately be short-lived and unable to sustain its growth. They fear it may collapse backwards into the all-to-prevalent, traditional pill-and-dependency medical model of care derived long ago from the marriage of the hospital and the alms house. Mason Mills’ documentary Revolutionizing Dementia Care may allay these doubts and concerns. In the words of the narrator, Brian LeBlanc—who is an individual with Alzheimer’s disease—the film’s primary purpose is to show “examples of how people living with dementia can still be empowered and engaged in long-term care communities by using the fundamental philosophy of person-centered care.” The video is overwhelmingly effective here. Indeed, it provides an extensive visual compendium of person-hood focused interventions—a useful guide for those seeking an introduction to this care philosophy and as well as those interacting with dementia-affected elders in long-term care settings and in the community. A vital message of the film is the news that our approaches to person-centered care now extend far beyond assisted living and full-care residential facilities. Community initiatives such as Dementia Friendly America introduce person-centered education and training to local policy makers, business leaders, owners, and service providers in cities, towns, and villages across the United States. In some cases, these programs are coordinated or folded within Age-Friendly City initiatives. (See https://www.dfamerica.org/). The introductory moments of Revolutionizing Dementia Care share the now-familiar statistics regarding the increasing prevalence of dementia worldwide. The staggering current figure—about 50 million people—prompted the World Health Organization in 2017 to initiate a global action plan regarding the human rights of people living with dementia. The report of the WHO initiative outlines core values at the heart of patient rights: empowerment, engagement, solidarity, equity, dignity, security, gender-sensitivity, “and a person-centered approach to promote respect and well-being” (WHO, 2017, p. 28). WHO has formally expressed a commitment to person-centered approaches that extends to the global level. The status level of the endorsement may assuage the fears of those who view person-centered care approaches as a mere seasonal fashion in the evolution of dementia care. Revolutionizing Dementia Care illustrates person-centered care strategies in actual operation across some of the best care facilities in the United States. Owners, staff, family members, and residents—in partnered fashion—live and/or work together to enable persons with dementia—mostly elders—to be understood and known for who they are, to emerge as fully as possible, as opposed to being viewed as remnants of their former selves. After viewing the video, I believe that even viewers well-informed about the ravages of dementia may be forced to revise their expectations of “possible self” capabilities still available to individuals living with dementia. John Zeisel, CEO of Hearthstone Alzheimer’s Care in Massachusetts, states that “The five things we know work for people with dementia that affect the way our brains work are diet, exercise, the amount of sleep we get, reducing stress, and meaning and purpose in life.” The film shares a dozen or more social, physical, environmental, and psychological interventions; many are directed at these five domains. Revolutionizing Dementia Care does not present research evidence evaluating individual changes in the five domains. It does, however, offer video snapshots of the shared excitement, commitment, wonder, and joy surrounding their associated care efforts—all of which are transferred to the viewer. I came away fully energized by this video tour. I share just a few of the examples I found amazing. One of the most remarkable efforts involves increasing the sense of personal bonding between “care partners” (staff members) and dementia-affected residents. Nicole Bays, Operations Director at Jill’s House in Bloomington, Indiana: “It was important to intentionally plan time to just get to know each other and to just spend time together. Our care partners eat meals with our residents.” Jan Bays, also of Jill’s House: “Why would you not sit down and have a meal with the people you’re taking care of? We’re asking these people to let us into the most private areas of their lives so to let them get to know us is amazing.” Outcomes? Dr. G. Allen Power, internationally recognized culture change leader, believes that the deepening of these relationships between residents and staff members has been a key to removing people from antipsychotic drugs. Establishing the desire in staff members to nurture closer relationships with elders requires education and training, of course. According to Victory Crenshaw, an administrator at Westminster Canterbury on Chesapeake Bay, Virginia: “. . . you’re supporting staff and helping them increase their skills and grow. You’re making it a pleasant place to live. It’s good for family to come and visit. You don’t have the staff turnover. In the long run, the return on investment is really good.” At Larmax Homes in Bethesda, Maryland, virtual reality technology is used to foster resident engagement and communication with others. A very special moment occurs when a care partner asks a resident to place a set of virtual reality goggles on her forehead (Figure 1): Resident uses the virtual reality goggles to swim with dolphins. CP: We’re going to look at some dolphins. Resident: Do I take my walker with me? CP: No. We’re just going to stay seated. How’s that feel? Resident: Oh, it’s a big fish. Oh, they’re big fish. A one, two, three, four, five, oh my gosh. Six. There’s too many of them. And there’s a baby underneath her and where is my hand. I can’t see it. CP: That’s amazing. Do you like it? Resident: Yes. I’ve never seen anything like it! Equine assisted therapy is also utilized at Larmax Homes. Owner Lori Larson notes that there is an “amazing body of knowledge about equine assisted therapy” that shows some success in reducing aggression and anxiety for short periods of time. We see four residents—including an elderly man Emmett—brushing a horse (Figure 2). Emmett (center) and friends: Equine assisted therapy. Lori explains, When Emmett first came to us, his wife had been passed away probably six months or so. He seemed fine. He had transitioned and everything else. And the first day we took him out to the horses, we found him rubbing the horse like this and he was saying “it’s going to be okay, Anne. It’s going to be okay.” Anne was his wife. And that was the only way we ever knew that he was struggling with her death. If it had not been for the horse we probably would have never known. We always have to find other ways to understand what people are thinking and give them an opportunity to connect and then share. It’s amazing. Viewers will find several other illustrations in Revolutionizing Dementia Care that are equally interesting. These include policies and practices usually associated with culture change care—engagement with children, animals, and plants (e.g., horticultural therapy); individualization and focus on individual strengths and choices; top-down innervation of person-care philosophy; personalized and group musical activity; freedom to express one’s own judgment as well as emotions; aromatherapy and sensory experiences, including touch via massage; predictable and enjoyable daily routines; continuity of family role engagement (e.g., as wife, mother, cook, or housekeeper); peer support groups; physical exercise linked to meaningful activities; and “bridging” opportunities to events and activities outside of the facility. Narrator Brian LeBlanc believes that while each intervention pursues specific outcomes, together they create an increased sense of normalcy that he seeks. In the closing scenes of the film, Susan Suchan, a dementia-affected individual, shares her own personal hopes: There’s this very fine line between “I do not want your pity” but “I do need your understanding”. Help me work with way my brain be go [sic]. Which means you need to get to know me. That’s care. It helps me remain the person I would want to be. I know what L-O-V-E means but I don’t feel that. So I lean into other words like dragonfly. The sound of birds. The ripple of sun on the water. People that come to my house with a smile on their face and say, “Hi, it’s great to see you.” How could you not feel good with that? —Susan Suchan, International Dementia Advocate and Mentor (1957–2018)

title: Among Hawks and Hummers
abstract: On Ontario's Sibley Peninsula, August was not too early for warblers and nuthatches, swallows and hawks to begin moving toward their winter ranges. They gathered at the southern tip, resting, feeding, waiting for clear skies and a fair wind. In a rocky clearing between Lake Superior and the forest, two rustic cabins housed the Thunder Cape Bird Observatory where I would work for the month. A college prof in my mid-fifties, I was anxious about doing well outside of a classroom.Birds have been important to me ever since the first great blue heron of my life levered itself up from a riverbed and lofted over my head, its wingspan greater than my height. Every spring, warblers have been bright postcards from warmer climates. I've fed chickadees perched on my hand—they apparently view a resting hiker as a supply wagon. Otherwise, birds have always been up there, out there, unreachable. At Thunder Cape I would stroke them and discover the astonishing density and depth of their feathers, the tininess of the bodies beneath.The staff was small. John, the only professional, quiet, always the teacher, talked about birds rather than himself. His wife, Mo, called herself Dragon Lady and told stories about a rowdy past. She outdid John in all dimensions—taller, broader, louder, brasher.Dean, slim and dignified, had arrived the day before me. He sported blond Rastafarian locks. In September he'd be a college senior. Jennifer, another volunteer, joined us mid-month. She looked to be in her thirties, tall and aloof, and came straight from a month or two at Long Point, a much larger observatory on Lake Erie. She carried a well-worn field guide and knew her birds cold, much better than I did.For six hours a day, from a platform above the beach, we stood watch, scanning lake and sky with binoculars, recording all birds seen and marking as migrants those headed south toward the nearest land, Michigan's Isle Royale. Every half hour two of us followed looped trails that led to clearings hung with mist nets, so fine they were nearly invisible. They caught songbirds; coarser nets occasionally snagged hawks. For the first week Mo taught me extraction techniques and John taught Dean. He learned faster, and I felt the big woman beside me twitch with impatience.The first bird I cleared solo was a Canada warbler. I held it up like a trophy and grinned at it. Dragonflies zoomed around us as if in celebration. I put it head-down in a soft cotton bag made by a Thunder Bay sewing club and tightened the drawstring. The bag calmed the bird the way a blindfold does a frightened horse. On the best days I had two or three bags hanging from my arm as I went on to the next net. It felt better than doing the Sunday Times crossword puzzle. In ink. In the tiny lab, John processed the birds—banded, aged, sexed, measured and weighed them, quickly, gently, while Dean and I took turns logging data. For weighing, John slipped the redstarts and thrushes on their heads into a toilet-paper tube with the bottom blocked with cardboard. Lifting them off the scale, he up-ended the tube over a clear plastic chute in the window, open to the outdoors. If the bird didn't emerge on its own, he tapped the tube and it slid out, shook its feathers into place and blurred away.“Down the tubes,” we'd say, flicking the cardboard that held a hesitant chickadee. “Sayonara” to the myrtle warbler that flew for all it was worth. To the many resident song sparrows, some of which we caught two or three times a day, we said, “Don't come back!”John watched Dean and me closely as we weighed, measured, and banded our first birds. Again, Dean learned faster. Sometimes my face was hot with embarrassment at how long the lab work took me. Jen, of course, needed no training and was almost as fast as John.Once or twice we found a hummingbird in a net. In John's hands it looked like an iridescent flower. He let them go as soon as he'd freed them: They were too fragile to band. Mo told us we'd make mistakes in the log. “White-out is your friend.” Other kinds of mistakes were more serious. A song sparrow sprang into the air from Dean's hands, flaring against lab windows above our reach, banging against the glass. Jen climbed onto the workbench and cupped the frantic creature in her hands.Some misfortunes were beyond our control. Dean and I found a mangled warbler in a net, feathers wet with blood.We called John, who extracted it without his usual finesse and tossed it into the bushes. He said it had been crushed by a deer. “They like the moisture,” he said, and told us to raise that net higher so the deer wouldn't notice caught birds.“Moisture?” I asked, after John left. Bird blood runs as red as ours. “Carnivorous deer?”Dean smiled his small smile. “Bambi the vampire.” Late in the month we caught sharp-shinned hawks, which slammed into our nets while streaking through the forest in pursuit of smaller birds. Usually snagged by the feet, they struggled mightily and sometimes got away. Strong, feisty creatures. First-years had heavily striped breasts and yellow eyes that would change to red by the next spring. Too large for our post-processing chute, hawks had to be released outside the lab.Why was it I felt an emotional tug when they flew? I tossed them up and they sank and then opened their wings and caught the air. Slow, powerful strokes, and the broad backs moved away sedately, at eye level. Weight lifted from my hands, from my whole body. As a child I flew in my dreams; was it not still possible? For a moment I believed so. One morning toward the end of the month, John and Mo went off in the launch to visit friends. Dean and I took it as a compliment, a vote of confidence in our new extracting and banding skills. We and Jen took turns, one of us taking the watch on the beach platform while the other two checked nets.I was on the platform when Dean bounded from the woods. “Do we have any scissors? Jen's got a sharpie in a tangle.” The mist nets were fine enough to be broken with our fingers, but hawk nets were tougher.“I have a jackknife,” I said. “Can you take the watch?”At the net, Jen looked uncharacteristically rattled. The sharpie was a mess. He'd got one wing involved and his feet were crossed in a bundle of mesh. He looked alert, eyes fierce. For some reason I took that yellow gaze as a challenge and put my jackknife back in my pocket.“Let me try,” I said to Jen. “You're burned out.”Feet first. I got one free, and the hawk immediately stuck it back into the net. “No, you don't,” I told him. I pulled it out again and started on the other. It took longer, but I felt calm. I had to free him; there was nobody else right there, right then. Who knew when John and Mo would be back? Maybe not until sundown. Maybe not until the next day.I concentrated, one strand at a time. The second foot was free. I breathed a sigh of relief. The wing would be easier.The wing wasn't easier. I stopped and looked at the sky, then back at the hawk. Imagined him as a scaled-up warbler. As I slid the last strand off, Dean pounded up with a pair of scissors.I held the hawk like an oversized ice-cream cone, my hand around his lower body with the legs pressed against it. I was so relieved I laughed. The hawk's head swiveled toward the sound, and I met his alien eyes. He tested my hold with a powerful wing-stroke that lifted my arm. So different from a songbird! The protocol for carrying hawks to the lab was different, too—we slid them into Pringle's potato-chip cans with holes in the bottom for air.I hesitated. He'd been in the net longer than I liked. “Should we just let him go?”The three of us assessed him. He looked fine—not droopy or trembling. So I Pringled him, which confirmed my guess at his gender: the larger female sharpies’ tails protruded from the tube by an inch or two, but this hawk slid neatly in until his tail disappeared.In the lab, Jen was angry. “They shouldn't have left us alone,” she said. “It's irresponsible.”“Right.” But I was glad, because freeing that hawk was a boost I badly needed. I'd been able to get him out when Jen and Dean couldn't. Finally, I'd done something right. A turning, like a shift from minor to major chord. My anxiety melted. I found myself held in an invisible net of bird flights, the air changed where they had flown, would fly. Other strands were made of song, pulses of sound that lifted me, a kind of talk that included me even though I couldn't speak its language. The trees listened too, and ferns vibrated. Among the community of species, I was one. Mo and I were clearing the table. She turned to me. “You closed the nets?” We volunteers had put them up for a few extra hours that afternoon.“Yes.” The disappointments of the afternoon prickled up. I'd had to close all the nets by myself, and had gotten skunked in the bargain—not even a recidivist song sparrow to bag. Dean and Jen had agreed to share the work, but he'd disappeared and she was snoring in her bunk.Never mind, I told myself. In a few minutes we'd all settle in for the nightly Scrabble game. Sporadic talk would bring us closer. We weren't friends—we'd probably never see each other once we left this place—but we were bound by the wilderness and our work in it and the importance of those things to us.Only one more day to go. Mo made cocoa and we settled around the kitchen table. It was a cool night, windy; in the dark bay beyond the window, the red light on the navigation buoy rose and fell. The forces of my ordinary life welled up around the little cabin, ready to reassert themselves. My legs swung out of the bunk and I was putting on my boots in the dark before I knew what I was doing, as if my body had gotten a command my mind hadn't heard about yet. I dressed quickly, found my headlamp by feel, and crept through the cabin like a cat burglar. The kitchen clock said five minutes past four. I closed the door silently.Cold outside. Now I knew where my body was going, and why. I argued back at it, trying to ease the clutch in my chest: I closed that net. I closed all the nets. I remembered doing it, the poles in my hands, the cloth strips. I pulled the nets down. I tied them.The tightness inside me didn't go away. My body was taking me to the farthest net. Normally I would have gone past John and Mo's cabin, but I took the long way around and kept my light off, finding my way by starlight.I closed them all.I reached the net. The rolled mesh hung low, its orange ties bright when I switched on my headlamp.Before I could relax, I saw farther on another net, hanging open. This was the double, the only double net in the whole study site. I'd been working with it for a month. How could I not have remembered?Moving forward, I pulled off my headlamp and flashed its beam over the second net, hoping, for the first time, to see it empty. Left untended since just before dinnertime. A bird caught for hours? Unthinkable.No birds. I took a breath.Two more steps, three. I saw something. It was so small it couldn't be a bird. It must be a leaf.It wasn't a leaf. I stopped in front of the tiny thing and felt blood pound in my ears.A hummingbird. It wasn't moving. I felt like flinging myself on the ground. Howling.I put the headlamp back on. Breathed deeply in and out, and focused on the bird. It was badly tangled. I looked at its feet, its wings. How could it be so tiny? I broke one net strand, then another.Stood with the hummingbird in my hand, the night deathly quiet around us. Then a breeze sprang up, and the lake sighed.I was numb. Poleaxed with shame.A thrush called somewhere in the dark forest. It would be light soon. For a moment I thought about burying the bird. No. I needed to pull the net down, tie it and leave. Later, John or Mo would wonder about the broken strands. Maybe they would ask what had happened. Whether they asked or not, I would tell them.Sick, I looked at the bird again, its iridescent feathers shimmering in my headlamp beam. I tossed it toward some bushes where it would fall out of sight. I watched to make sure it did—the thought of John discovering a dead hummer was mortifying.The arc of its fall reversed and it flew away.I stood, fighting disbelief. Finally understanding: The warmth of my hands had revived it. I rolled up the net and stumbled back to the cabin. With any luck the hummer had been there only a few minutes. I talked myself into believing this. If it had been hanging there all night it surely would have died. So it must have been active very early.By the light of day I knew I couldn't face Mo's wrath, John's disgust. So I said nothing, did my work. If Dean or Jen noticed I didn't join their conversations while we stood the watch, they would think it was because of the sadness of leaving the next day. And it was that, too. But now I carried another burden. I'd been tested, and I'd failed. Early in the month a couple of backpackers had asked John if they could camp overnight in the room at the top of a 50-meter tower in the forest behind the cabins. Great idea. I'd meant to sleep up there myself. I did so at my last night on the peninsula, perhaps in symbolic recognition of my new distance from the good-hearted, trustworthy people in the cabins below.Carrying my sleeping bag and a thermos of coffee, I climbed above the dark woods. Up there, the sun was just setting. Large windows showed me a cloud factory: Wind coming over the lake was forced to rise up a rocky cliff, becoming visible as the water condensed out at the top. The cliff looked as if it were steaming toward the lake, trailing a thin cloud.The night sky treated me kindly. Northern Lights pulsed and shivered, shadowy white sheets hung out to dry. Knees against my chest, I stared at them. How should I regard something so lovely? What was my relationship, now, to the Lights, to the warblers and thrushes I'd handled, to the owl I heard among the moon-shadows below me? To the porcupine I'd seen beside the path, standing, a nursing kit at her quill-free, black belly? What could I say to the coming dawn? My failure mystified me. Not closing that net could have meant a dead hummingbird. Or more than one. How could I have overlooked an open net?I tried out excuses. It was dusk, and the mist nets were so fine even birds didn't see them.But I was not a bird. And I'd known the net was there. There was something wrong with me.No, I'd made a mistake—as Mo had predicted we all would.The full moon rose and washed out the Lights, dimmed the stars. Yet the Big Dipper still hung in one window and Cassiopeia in the other. My mind drifted slowly with them. Constellations were a museum of stories, millennia of tales about failure and recovery, shame and resilience.I lay in my sleeping bag and gathered the best moments of the month—the thrill of freeing my first bird, the satisfaction of extricating the sharp-shinned hawk. How I'd felt connected to the peninsula, to the birds I'd held and those I hadn't, how I'd been held in turn by all their songs, by the hosts of leaves they inhabited, by the forest and its understory.That morning, Dean, master of simplicity, had said, “I'm glad I got up today.”I kept my own kind of watch, and then I slept.

abstract: John Muir Newsletter summer 1993 university of the pacific volume 3, number 3 JOHN MUIR IN THE ION BASIN by Laurel Bemis (Editor's note: a Stockton resident and recent graduate of the University of the Pacific, the author prepared this paper in a course offered by UOP's history department, "John Muir and the American Environment. " Excerpts from the John Muir Papers at UOP are used by permission of the Muir-Hanna Trust.) John Muir left New York on April 20, 1911 on a voyage that would fulfill his lifetime dream to travel to South America. One of his main reasons for visiting the Amazon basin at this late stage in his life was his desire to see ancient araucaria trees in their original habitat. Nicknamed the "monkey puzzle" tree, its spiny bark prevents monkeys from climbing it. Muir felt that it was one of the most important trees in existence because it has survived many geological periods. He was prepared to travel any distance, by boat and by foot if necessary, to view this biological wonder. Although he was seventy-four years old at the time of his trip, it was alleged that he could still walk twenty-five or thirty miles a day. ' On August 27, he wrote in his journal at noon that he was less than two hundred miles from the mouth of the Amazon. It took about an hour of cautious maneuvering by the ship's crew before dropping anchor because of the shifting delta currents which made charts unreliable. The following day, Muir viewed the land surrounding the Amazon for the first time and noted "Many magnificent dome-headed giant trees looming in most imposing grandeur above the crowded multitudes of palms." 2 That afternoon he arrived at Para and later visited the city park. He wrote in great detail about the various ferns, palms, and lilies of the garden, citing their scientific names as well as intricate measurements of their leaves, height, and other specifications. On September 1, Muir rose at four o'clock in the morning to begin a boat trip up the great river. In some places the over-leaning trees were so close he could almost touch them. As he traveled he noticed a large number of white-flowered trees, about seventy-five feet in height, and many other trees of the same type with red flowers. Palms grew scarce after about 200 miles above Para. His journal describes the palm-thatched houses of the Indians that could be seen every few miles. Rubber was collected at these small settlements to trade for Portuguese tobacco, coffee, coal oil, calico, and other products. During the night, he reported that a swarm of Brazilian mosquitoes came aboard and "invaded the dining room, where we were seated at the tables, causing lively slapping and clapping, in defending ourselves from their stings. The clapping was so continuous that a stranger might fancy that a speaker was being cheered. The dead mosquitoes were piled on the table-cloth at the side of each plate and each [person] seemed to be anxious to make [such] good use of the sport that he seemed to enjoy it, each claiming a greater number of the game than their neighbors." 3 A day later, free of mosquitoes, the travelers passed through a more colorful crowd. "A good many butterflies, moths, dragonflies...are enlivening the air," Muir wrote. He also described the houses which belonged to Portuguese tradesmen, which were large with red-tiled roofs, and had big herds of cattle on the surrounding (continued on page 6) 1 ■ SIGNIFICANT BOOKS ON THE ENVIRONMENT SELECTED Which books do environmentalists consider to have been the most significant so far published? Robert Meridith of the Pennsylvania Groundwater Policy Education Project at Pennsylvania State University has conducted a survey to determine which writings have been the most influential in shaping the environmental movement. A sample of over two hundred environmental authors, scientists, activists and government officials selected Sand Country Almanac by Aldo Leopold, published in 1949, as the book that had been most important in leading to the emergence of the environmental movement. The other books which made the list, in order of their selection, were Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962); Status of the World (an annual publication of the Worldwatch Institute); Paul Ehrlich's Tlie Population Bomb (1968); Henry David Thoreau's Walden (1854)]_Roderick Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (1967); E.F. Schumacher's Small is Beautiful (1973); Barry Commoner's The Closing Circle (1971); and Limits to Growth (1972) by Donella Meadows, Dennis Meadows, Jorgen Randers, and William Behrens. The John Muir Newsletter invites its readers and subscribers to make up their own list. Which books have most interested you and affected your views on the environment? EWS AND NOTES Gordon Strain of Martinez, who sold some of his land for inclusion in the John Muir Nature Trial, died during a dedication ceremony of the land in June. He suffered a heart attack and was taken from the dedication site by helicopter to the John Muir Medical Center in Walnut Creek, where he died. In 1991 Strain had sold 186 acres of Mount Wanda, named after Muir's older daughter, to the National Park Service. That area offers a spectacular view of Martinez, Mount Diablo, and the Sacramento- San Joaquin Delta, and is covered by native oak, bay and fruit and nut trees. The John Muir Newsletter is indebted to Mr. Strain, and its staff are saddened by the loss. He was determined that his land become part of the John Muir heritage for Californians and others to enjoy. One of our readers has sent a note of encouragement which we wish to share. Elizabeth Pomeroy of Pasadena writes that "... the Newsletter is excellent and I encourage you to continue! It brings far flung J.M. scholars together and benefits all our work." Please send in your thoughts—kudos or criticisms—and we will be pleased to publish them. UPDATE ON MUIR BOOK Although delayed, the book John Muir: Life and Work, edited by Sally Miller and containing papers from the 1990 Muir Conference, is still on track and will be published sometime this fall, according to the publisher, University of New Mexico Press. Limbaugh This Newsletter is printed on recycled paper. A NEW LOOK AT AN IMPORTANT BOOK Linnie Marsh Wolfe, Son of the Wilderness: The Life of John Muir. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1945. Reviewed by Char Miller, Trinity University, San Antonio, Texas (Editor's Note: Virtually evety student of John Muir's life turns to Son of the Wilderness by Linnie Marsh Wolfe, whatever other biographies of Muir they may read. So it seemed a good idea to have one of today's major environmental historians take another look at the Wolfe biography almost fifty years after its publication.) Linnie Marsh Wolfe loved John Muir, loved his "flashing blue eyes," his lyrical language, and the wilderness ideals he represented; she also adored the Sierra, that v Range of Light' he did so much to illuminate through thought, word, and deed. Even when she dedicated Son of the Wilderness to her husband, Robert Wolfe, and the shared joy they felt while tramping through "the meadows and groves and along the trails of the Yosemite," she had her mind on that majestic valley's most famed interpreter: in all sorts of ways Muir had made their experiences possible. Wolfe was nothing if not grateful, as her text amply demonstrates. By immersing herself in Muir's life, for example, by soaking in his correspondence and journals, she was able to craft what amounts to a first-person narrative, the autobiography he never wrote for himself. The book, she believed, would have the added effect of lifting "a few veils that have obscured his rich life among men, thus . . . making him somewhat more than a disembodied voice crying in the wilderness" (vii). For these efforts, Wolfe was awarded the 1946 Pulitzer Prize for biography. The choice, in retrospect, seems odd, for the book's reception was mixed. Although the Kirkus reviewer found it an "inspiring story,"1 and Richard Hofstadter praised it as the "definitive study of Muir's odd career,"2 many other prominent journals and critics were less impressed. The New Yorker, among others, was disappointed: "Very earnest, very well documented, and considering the material the author had to work with, rather unforgivably dull."3 More significant still were the concerns about the work's literary propriety and provenance. As Leonard Dubkin observed, "Mrs. Wolfe has let her love for the memory of John Muir overshadow her critical judgement, and the result is none too happy" or could in fact be called an unhappy result, flowing as well from the text's status as an "authorized" life: "one should never write a biography with the subject's daughters looking over one's shoulder."4 Linnie Marsh Wolfe was a kept woman. Nearly a half century later, these and other flaws seem all the more pronounced. Wolfe's documentation, for instance, is haphazard—some direct quotations are cited by sources, many others are not. title: The Womb of Virtuality: From Plato to Posthumanism
venue: PAJ A Journal of Performance and Art
abstract: A peril of writing about new technology: when I started working on this essay, Mark Zuckerberg had just announced the rebranding of Facebook into Meta, signaling his desire to engineer, monetize, and control the vast networked virtual something called “the metaverse”; when I completed a draft of it, the multinational conglomerate Siemens had teamed up with the technology titan NVIDIA to pioneer a form of the metaverse geared to industrial applications; and by the time I had submitted it for consideration, thousands of Meta employees were in the process of being laid off following another massive quarterly loss from Reality Labs (Meta’s metaverse-creation division). It was a familiar cycle to anyone who follows virtual reality, which has long obeyed laws of hype and humiliation. But fixation on such booms and busts should not occlude recognition of the real progress being made. The metaverse, which under one name or another (cyberspace, the matrix, OASIS, etc.) has been a recurring dream at least since William Gibson’s novel Neuromancer (1984), was edging closer to realization even as it was disappearing from headlines. It was edging closer because the development of a necessary component, artificial intelligence, was accelerating at staggering speed. If the great leap forward in AI that began in 2022 temporarily eclipsed the construction of the metaverse, it also provided a key to its viability.You, dear reader, will have a better idea of where all this is headed than I do as I type these words. But one thing at least is clear: VR has developed far enough circa 2023 that one can begin to survey not just the trees but the forest. This essay identifies a basic term—“presence”—as central to the medium of VR. And it identifies a basic distinction between humanist and posthumanist approaches as critical to understanding the medium’s shape and direction. To understand all this, it will help to return to N. Katherine Hayles’s 1999 monograph How We Became Posthuman and then to turn yet further back, all the way to Plato’s cave. This journey will then set the stage for the examination of humanist and posthumanist approaches to aesthetics, which will be chiefly exemplified by two artworks: Chris Milk’s Evolution of Verse (2015) and Jacolby Satterwhite’s Domestika (2017).In retrospect, Hayles’s groundbreaking study How We Became Posthuman seems to have been right about almost everything. But it was wrong about this: it underestimated the persistence of presence in our virtual age.Hayles’s book describes a world in which presence and absence, the shadow play that had come to define Western thought at least since Plato, was rapidly giving way to a dynamic dance of pattern and randomness. (The former dialectic Hayles dubs “materiality,” the latter “information.”) VR in particular, for Hayles, illuminates this broader epistemic shift “toward pattern/randomness and away from presence/absence,” and thus might be considered a technology of information par excellence.1 “The technologies of virtual reality,” she writes, “with their potential for full-body mediation, further illustrate the kind of phenomena that foreground pattern and randomness and make presence and absence seem irrelevant.” Why “irrelevant”? Because in situations where “the relevant boundaries for interaction are defined less by the skin than by the feedback loops connecting body and simulation in a technobio-integrated circuit . . . questions about presence and absence do not yield much leverage.” Most centrally, VR is a medium of information, of code, of noise and signal, with materiality a remnant of an older, pre-digital discourse—not quite eradicable from the medium, perhaps, but also not significantly constitutive. According to this logic, VR materiality should be viewed as a kind of red herring, one that threatens to mislead those too bound up with pre-posthuman ways of thinking to learn to read the code behind the screens.Is talk about VR “presence,” then, just a mask or a misdirection for processes of information? Is VR presence like the headlights and tailfins on a 1950s Cadillac—alluring, but not what’s going on beneath the hood?No. Presence persists, now in a dance with information. And nowhere is this persistence and this dance more clearly exemplified than in VR.It may help to recall some history. What is now called “presence” in virtual technology was once dubbed “telepresence,” a word with roots back in an article written for Omni magazine back in 1980. In that piece, the MIT cognitive scientist Marvin Minsky coined the term to speculate about a future in which technologies would allow people to use bodies remotely. “The biggest challenge to developing telepresence,” he cautioned, “is achieving that sense of ‘being there.’ Can telepresence be a true substitute for the real thing?”2 Minsky’s answer to his own question was an emphatic “yes.” In the ensuing decade or so, the “tele-” prefix largely dropped away, and presence came to be widely regarded as a central element—perhaps the central aspect—of the emergent medium. In 1992, one of the premiere journals of virtual technology began publication out of MIT; its title is Presence.Matthew Lombard and Theresa Ditton, two leading researchers into virtual presence, argue for six basic aspects of the term when applied to VR: social richness (does the medium feel personal?), realism (do the representations seem accurate?), transportation (do you feel like you are really “there,” or that it is “here,” or that “we are together”?), immersion (are you engrossed?), social action with the medium (can you interact with the medium?), and the medium as social actor (can the medium interact with you?). Abstracting from these, Lombard and Ditton further identify the common thread that tied all these aspects together and derived from it a general definition. Presence, they conclude, is “the perceptual illusion of nonmediation.”3It is hard not to be struck by the irony of the fact that the term “presence,” with its longstanding connotations of authenticity and truth, has come, in VR discourse, to be associated with precisely the opposite: with illusion. But there is also a deeper idea at play here, driven at once by a business model and a romance. It is a dream that through the “perceptual illusion of nonmediation,” genuine connection, actual experience, some feeling of truly being there might be engineered into existence. Zuckerberg would make such ideas company policy in 2021 when he announced the rebranding of Facebook into Meta. “The defining quality of the metaverse will be a feeling of presence—like you are right there with another person or in another place,” he wrote in the Founder’s Letter of that year.4 “Feeling truly present with another person is the ultimate dream of social technology.” And as Meta began seriously engineering its version of the metaverse (aided by an in-house project, launched in 2021, called the Presence Platform), “presence” continued to be the keystone of the edifice. According to Nick Clegg, who went from being Deputy Prime Minister of the United Kingdom to Vice President of Global Affairs and Communications at Meta, the metaverse’s “defining quality will be a feeling of presence, like you are right there with another person or in another place.”5 This feeling of presence, writes Clegg, will be about much more than merely being “right there”; it will also be about “enriching our experience” and digitally reproducing and thereby strengthening the social relations of analogue life.This romance of VR’s power to deepen human connection is shared even by some who lament the uses to which it is being put. VR pioneer Jaron Lanier, for instance, urges his audiences to delete their social-media accounts, calling social-media companies “behavior-modification empires.”6 At the same time, he celebrates VR’s capacity for interpersonal connection in terms similar to those of Zuckerberg and Clegg. He hopes that, properly deployed, VR will teleport its participants to a “shared, waking state,” an “intentional, communicative, collaborative dream,” which will “hopefully” provide “a path to increased empathy” for individuals and society as a whole—on a global scale. “Virtual reality was and remains a revelation,” he concludes. “There’s a moment that comes when you notice that even when everything changes, you are still there, at the center, experiencing whatever is present.”Presence, then, is more than a just technical term for VR. It gestures toward an unquantifiable object of deeper desire: a gesture toward the actual, the true, the connected, the shared, the deeply experienced and felt—all mediated by a machine that erases all traces of its own mediation. This is why the old complaint that VR is escapist misses the deeper longing of the medium, a longing not so much for escape as for return.Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, predictably enough, played an important role in the programming, theorizing, and fantasizing of early VR. Like others of my generation, my own first experience of VR took place inside a CAVE, or “Cave Automatic Virtual Environment,” an early form of VR that relied on surround-screen projection technology that immersed the user in an interactive audio-visual cube. The technology, invented in 1992 and still in wide use, was described by its inventors as “a reference to ‘The Simile of the Cave’ found in Plato’s Republic, in which the philosopher discusses inferring reality (ideal forms) from projections (shadows) on the cave wall.”7In the wake of Luce Irigaray’s reading of the Allegory in Speculum of the Other Woman (1974), one can no longer ignore the gendered connotations of Plato’s Allegory: the Cave is, in her words, “a metaphor of the inner space, of the den, the womb or hystera [uterus].”8 It is a female space inhabited strictly by humans whose implicit gender is masculine; humans with their “heads forward, eyes front, genitals aligned, fixed in a straight direction and always straining forward, in a straight line. A phallic direction, a phallic line, a phallic time, backs turned on origin.” This line—this straight line—points directly from Plato to VR. If one needed a demonstration, in cartoonish form, of the application of Irigaray’s reading for VR circa 2016, one could do no better than to search up that notorious photo posted by Zuckerberg on Facebook of a conference auditorium of seated, suited men hooked up to Oculus headsets (“heads forward, eyes front, genitals aligned”) while the chairman strides down the aisle.9VR reminds us that love and loathing of the womb is Plato’s poisoned gift to modern technology. title: Illuminating Iridescence: Nature’s Shimmering Marriage of Geometry and Light
abstract: One moment it resembles a ruby, the next a topaz, then an emerald, and then again gleaming gold. —Charles Waterton, Wanderings in South America What ruse do ruby-topaz hummingbirds (described in the quotation above), Karner blue butterflies, Queen of the Night tulips, and countless other glittering species employ to escape predators, find mates, claim territory, camouflage themselves, and communicate? In a marriage of geometry and light, they use a hue trick called iridescence to change color as the angle of view or illumination changes. An iridescent ruby-topaz hummingbird (Chrysolampis mosquitus) shines like pure gold. Photograph: Ysmad. “Iridescence is nature’s color magic,” according to Karen Jameson, author of Time to Shine: Celebrating the World’s Iridescent Animals. “Blink and you might miss it.” Many bird feathers, insect wings, reptile and fish scales, and animal furs have special structures or layers that shift light in different directions, blending the reflections into each other. The iridescence that makes birds like peacocks and butterflies such as Karner blues shimmer results from nanostructures so complex researchers are only beginning to discover their secrets. They are finding that iridescence may inspire such technological advances as energy-efficient reflective displays and imaging techniques that hold promise in early disease detection. When light strikes a peacock feather, we see thousands of glittering spots. The feathers of pheasants, birds of paradise, hummingbirds and many other species create iridescence using the same trick of light. Photograph: Bernard Spragg. Scientists have learned that there are two main ways color is produced in animals: pigments and structures. Cells called melanocytes produce pigments like melanin, which is responsible for black and brown coloration. “Structural color,” however, comes not from pigments but from the way light bounces off microscopic surfaces. Iridescence is an example of structural color. As iridescent birds or insects move, microscopic crystalline structures amplify certain wavelengths of light, depending on a viewer’s angle. “It is interesting to note that the special qualities of iridescent animal colors… were first mentioned and discussed by physicists,’” writes Hilda Simon in The Splendor of Iridescence: Structural Colors in the Animal World. Indeed, physicist Sir Isaac Newton drew attention to the peacock’s iridescent colors in his Treatise on Optics, published in 1704. “The finely colored feathers of some birds, and especially those of peacocks,” he wrote, “do in the very same part of the feather appear of several colors in several positions of the eye, after the very same manner that thin plates were found to do.” Newton had the right idea. The regular structures that produce iridescence are submicroscopic. With the advent of the electron microscope in 1931, greatly enlarged views of those tiny plate-like structures led to a new understanding of the phenomenon. It all, or mostly, comes down to geometry, scientists have found. Changes in viewing geometry “can dramatically alter the appearance of iridescent colors, producing considerable changes in hue, intensity, or both,” state Melissa Meadows, of the University of Florida, and Stephanie Doucet, of the University of Windsor, in the 2009 Interface Focus paper “Iridescence: A functional perspective.” Iridescent colors, Meadows and Doucet report, “appear brilliant and saturated at optimal viewing geometries. When the viewing geometry changes, however, the iridescence can disappear entirely.” A bird with brilliant blue feathers, such as the common grackle, seen from another angle, may not look blue at all. Rainbow boa (Epicrates cenchria); this iridescent species is native to Central and South America in areas such as the Amazon River basin. Photograph: Bernard DuPont. Light scattering by living things is “usually coherent, with all the outgoing light waves in lock-step,” write Justin Marshall, a neuroscientist at the University of Queensland, and coauthors in Color in Nature. “An example is thin layering of materials that affect how fast light travels through them. If the layers are very regular, reflections are iridescent—their apparent color changes with the angle of view.” The thin layers are a type of photonic crystal, according to Color in Nature, “a term that sounds straight out of science fiction but refers to nanoscale structures with a regular geometry. Almost all naturally occurring photonic crystals are built by living organisms. Whenever you see a brilliant blue on a living thing, or an iridescent flash, or a bright metallic sheen… photonic crystals are responsible.” Animals have flashed with iridescence since the time of the dinosaurs, scientists working in China recently discovered. The researchers unearthed a duck-size dinosaur called Caihong juji. In Mandarin, its name means "rainbow with the big crest"; the dinosaur lived some 161 million years ago and sported iridescent feathers. Caihong juji is the oldest known iridescent species. Biologists are not sure why iridescence evolved, but they are finding new answers by studying 13,000-year-old beetle or weevil fossils. Camouflage and signaling mates and predators may be primary reasons. Two fossilized weevils from the late Pleistocene, found on the shores of a lake in Switzerland, are offering insights. Researchers used ultra-bright X-rays to learn when the ancient insects evolved the tiny crystalline structures that make them iridescent. Using electron microscopes, synchrotron X-ray scattering and optical modeling techniques to identify the crystal nanostructures in the fossil weevils—whose blue and green hues are like those of modern weevils—the biologists revealed a diamond-like pattern in the scales. The results were published in April 2020, in Biology Letters. Vinod Kumar Saranathan, of Yale-NUS College in Singapore, and colleagues discovered that the green and blue structural colors of the weevils have been the same for at least 13,000 years. “We compared our fossil samples to modern beetle wings of the same genus and found them to be very similar,” said Saranathan, who led the research in collaboration with paleobiologists Maria McNamara and Luke McDonald, of University College Cork, in Ireland. “That’s a long time for insects, nearly 50,000 generations, and the color has not changed.” The researchers believe the weevils’ green color first appeared as camouflage millions of years ago when the beetles began eating plant leaves. Over time, the weevils likely used iridescent colors as a way of signaling potential mates and warding off predators. “We demonstrate that—despite their widespread geographic and taxonomic distribution—three-dimensional photonic crystals appear to have evolved only once in weevils, in the common ancestor of a clade comprising the current subfamilies Entiminae and Cyclominae [broad-nosed weevils],” the scientists report. Throughout history, iridescence has fascinated humans from Aristotle, writing more than 2000 years ago in his Historia animalium, to today’s scientists in fields from optical physics to evolutionary biology and beyond. In the 2009 paper “Iridescence: Views from many angles,” in Interface Focus, Melissa Meadows and colleagues state that “scientists from a variety of disciplines study the optics, development, heritability, chemical makeup, origin, evolution, functions and biomimetic technological applications of naturally occurring iridescent colors.” Despite what Meadows calls a longstanding interest in iridescence, basic questions remain about its function, development, and evolution. That conclusion led to a conference at Arizona State University: “Iridescence: More than meets the eye.” The meeting attracted 90 participants from 12 countries; the attendees represented photonics, evolutionary biology, special effects rendering, developmental biology, materials science, education, architecture, and other fields. The conference participants agreed that a large knowledge gap exists in how iridescent nanostructures develop in organisms. “These developmental processes must be extremely precise because even small construction errors, on the order of only 20 nanometers, can produce changes in coloration,” state Meadows and colleagues. “We are just beginning to investigate the biological, chemical, and physical mechanisms that allow organisms to produce such highly organized, tiny structures.” Certain taxa, the scientists determined, may be more likely to display iridescence because of the material composition and development of their outer layers or certain environmental conditions. In beetles and butterflies, the cuticle is composed of layers of chitin that are iridescent. But "we know little, if anything, about the development of these structures in organisms other than insects and birds,” lament Meadows and colleagues. “Given the diversity of organisms that are iridescently colored… it is essential that we examine iridescent structures in more types of organisms.” In many examples, iridescence evolved in response to sexual selection, say the researchers. “There is growing evidence that iridescent coloration influences mate choice in certain species and may be an indicator of individual quality or condition,” according to Meadows. For instance, peacocks spread their iridescent feathers to attract peahens. The feathers are adorned with distinct color patterns, a stunning visual display. By showcasing their attractiveness through their flashy feathers, peacocks hope to catch the attention of potential mates. An ocellated turkey (Meleagris ocellata) in Tikal, Peten, Guatemala, glimmers with iridescence. Photograph: Charles J. Sharp. Iridescence is about more than conspicuous courtship displays, however. “Iridescent coloration can also function as camouflage, warning coloration, or as species recognition signals,” states Meadows. “Structures that produce iridescent coloration may also have noncommunicative functions such as enhancing water repellency, friction reduction, and thermoregulation.” The rainbow boa’s iridescent scales, for example, help the snake slither through tight spaces. The iridescent fur of the golden mole of South Africa allows this blind mammal to swim through sand as it moves through riverbanks and semidesertic areas. Iridescence is found in at least 14 species of mammals, including golden moles, according to Jessica Dobson, of Ghent University, and her colleagues. They report in September 2025, in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface, that species including the African grass rat, the African marsh rat, and the giant otter shrew are iridescent. The results "suggest that iridescence in mammals is more common than originally thought," says Dobson. A flashy rainbow beetle in Rock Creek Park, Washington, DC, United States. Photograph: Katja Schultz. Hummingbirds are among the best-known iridescent species, shimmering in a range of colors. “Hummingbirds… seem to have a luminescence of their own, almost as though they are lighted up from inside,” muses Simon in The Splendor of Iridescence. These tiny birds, such as the blue-chinned sapphire, crimson topaz, and ruby-topaz, are often compared with jewels. “Of all the colors found in the animal kingdom, the gleaming, glittering 'rainbow hues' are without a doubt the most eye-catching and attractive,” Simon states. Biologist Thomas White, of the University of Sydney, in Australia, would agree. In a paper on illuminating the evolution of iridescence published in the June 2018 issue of Trends in Ecology and Evolution, he writes that “structural coloration is capable of generating the extreme perceived brightness and chromaticity that characterizes the most striking visual displays in the world." The Karner blue butterfly, a resident of pine barrens where wild blue lupine grows, is an iridescent member of the Lycaenid family. Photograph: Paul Labus, The Nature Conservancy, Indiana. Among them is the luster of the national bird of Nepal, the Impeyan pheasant. Its iridescence is “of such breathtaking brilliance that older zoologists felt moved to give it the name Lophophorus resplendens, resplendent crest-bearer,” states Simon. The bird, which has a small crest of feathers on its head, was renamed Lophophorus impejanus after Lady Impey, the wife of a nineteenth century British officer. Lady Impey was so dazzled by the pheasant that she had several transported to England, where all efforts failed to tame this wild bird of the high Himalayan Mountains. The emerald swallowtail (Papilio palinurus), also called the emerald peacock or green-banded peacock, shimmers with iridescence. Photograph: D. Gordon E. Robertson. Some 7000 miles from the Himalayas, the Albany Pine Bush Preserve, just outside Albany, New York, is a mecca for another iridescent species, the federally endangered Karner blue butterfly (Lycaeides melissa samuelis). Karner blues are found in inland pine barrens in New York, New Hampshire, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Ohio. The Albany Pine Bush Preserve is one of the largest of 20 such pine barrens left in the world. It may be the best remaining example of this ecosystem, say scientists such as Neil Gifford, an ecologist and conservation director at the preserve. On a June visit, I go walkabout to explore hillsides covered with blue lupines in full bloom. Wild blue lupine (Lupinus perennis) is the only native lupine in New York State. In the Pine Bush, wild lupine blooms in open areas of pitch pine-scrub oak. Today, spiky blue flowers dot the landscape as far as the eye can see. That’s good news for the Pine Bush’s Karner blue butterflies. In their caterpillar stage, wild lupine is the Karner blues’ only food. The iridescent purple ‘Queen of the Night' tulip in the Wrocław University Botanical Garden, in Poland. Photograph: Agnieszka Kwiecien, Nova. Diminutive Karner blues have wingspans of 1.3 inches or less, with the upper wing surfaces of the males an iridescent gray-blue. A tiny, bright flash in the summer sun heralds the arrival of a male Karner blue as he lands on a lupine flower, his wings glinting. “As the day warms and the dew evaporates,” reflects Gifford, “Karners take flight, their wings shimmering across the lupine as hundreds of adults search for mates. The iridescence of freshly eclosed butterflies [those just emerged from a chrysalis] is spectacular,” he says, but gradually wanes as the butterflies come to the end of their short, 5-day life spans. Pine barrens with blue lupines and Karner blues were historically maintained by natural forces such as wildfires. Human impacts, including fire suppression, have resulted in the disappearance of many of these habitats. At the Albany Pine Bush, open butterfly habitat is managed through controlled burns that keep trees and shrubs in check. The Karner blue is also threatened by with wings are to scientists have found.
